syn_none.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The reliable prediction of the temporal behavior of complex systems is key in numerous scientific fields. This strong interest is however hindered by modeling issues: often, the governing equations describing the physics of the complex systems under consideration are not accessible or, if known, the solution of the governing equations might require a computational time incompatible with the prediction time constraints. Not surprisingly, approximating complex systems in a generic functional format and informing the generic functional format ex-nihilo from available observations has become common practice in the age of machine learning, as illustrated by the numerous successful examples based on deep neural networks. However, generalizability of the deep neural networks models, margins of guarantee and the impact of data are often overlooked or examined mainly by relying on prior knowledge of the physics. We tackle these issues from a different viewpoint, by adopting a curriculum learning strategy. In curriculum learning, the dataset is structured such that the training process starts from simple samples towards more complex samples in order to favor convergence and generalization. The curriculum learning concept has been developed and successfully applied in robotics and control of complex systems. Here, we apply this curriculum learning concept for the learning of complex dynamical systems in a systematic way. First, leveraging insights from the ergodic theory, we assess the amount of data sufficient for a-priori guaranteeing a faithful model of the physical complex systems and thoroughly investigate the impact of the training set and the structure of the training set on the quality of long-term predictions. Based on that, we consider entropy as a metric of complexity of the dataset; we show how an informed design of the training set based on the analysis of the entropy significantly improves the resulting models in terms of generalizability, and provide insights on the amount of data and the choice of data required for an effective data-driven modeling.
syn_none.coling::7876816d-0ac2-4404-b2bf-deeaa0b7:
The CII 158 microns line is the most important coolant of the interstellar
medium in galaxies but substantial variations are seen from galaxy to galaxy.
The main source of the CII emission at a galactic scale is still poorly understood.
Previous studies of the CII emission in galaxies have a resolution of several
kpc or more so the observed CII emission is an average of different ISM components.
The aim of this work is to study, for the first time, the CII emission at the
scale of a spiral arm. We want to investigate the origin of the CII line and the use of the CII line as a tracer of star formation. We present CII observations and OI observations of a
segment of a spiral arm of M~31 using the Infrared Space Observatory. The CII
emission is compared with tracers of neutral gas (CO, HI) and tracers of star formation
(H\alpha, Spitzer 24 mu.) The similarity of the CII emission with the H\alpha and 24
mu images is striking when smoothed to the same resolution, whereas the
correlation with the neutral gas is much weaker. The CII cooling rate per H
atom increases dramatically from ~2.7e-26 ergs/s/atom in the border of the map
to ~ 1.4e-25 ergs/s/atom in the regions of star formation. The CII/FIR(42-122)
ratio is almost constant at 2%, a factor 3 higher than typically quoted.
However, we do not believe that M~31 is unusual. Rather, the whole-galaxy
fluxes used for the comparisons include the central regions where the CII/FIR
ratio is known to be lower and the resolved observations neither isolate a
spiral arm nor include data as far out in the galactic disk as the observations
presented here. A fit to published PDR models yields a plausible average
solution of G_0~100 and n~3000 for the PDR emission in the regions of star
formation in the spiral arm of M31.
syn_none.coling::1a16d27a-89fc-4df9-8b4f-cf2532a8: We study a two-dimensional (2D) tight-binding model of a topological crystalline insulator (TCI) protected by rotation symmetry. The model is built by stacking two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers which transform under conjugate representations of the rotation group, e.g. $p_\pm$ orbitals. Despite the apparent similarity of the model to the Kane-Mele model, the model does not host stable gapless surface states. Nevertheless the model exhibits topological responses including the appearance of quantized fractional charge bound to rotational defects (disclinations) and the pumping of angular momentum in response to threading an elementary magnetic flux, which topological responses are described by a mutual Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective gauge field corresponding to the rotation symmetry. In addition, we show that although the filled bands of the model do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation, this obstruction is removed upon the addition of appropriate atomic orbitals, which addition implies fragile topology. As a result, the response of the model can be derived by representing the model as a superposition of atomic orbitals with positive and negative integer coefficients. Following the analysis of the model, which model serves as a prototypical example of 2D TCIs protected by rotation symmetry, we show that all TCIs protected by point group symmetries which do not have protected surface states are either atomic insulators or fragile phases. Remarkably, this result implies that gapless surface states exist in free electron systems if and only if there is a stable Wannier obstruction. We then use dimensional reduction to map the problem of classifying 2D TCIs protected by rotation symmetry to a zero-dimensional (0D) problem which problem is then used to obtain the complete non-interacting classification of such TCIs as well as the reduction of this classification in the presence of interactions.
syn_none.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243: We introduce a new artificial intelligence (AI) approach called, the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS). The Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate uses selected attributes from objects in various domains (e.g. chess problems, classical music, renowned artworks) and recombines the selected attributes in such a way as to generate new attributes that can then, in principle, be used to create novel objects of creative value to humans relating to any one of the source domains. The Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate allows some of the burden of creative content generation to be passed from humans to machines. The approach was tested in the domain of chess problem composition. We used the approach to automatically compose numerous sets of chess problems based on attributes extracted and recombined from chess problems and tournament games by humans, renowned paintings, computer-evolved abstract art, photographs of people, and classical music tracks. The quality of these generated chess problems was then assessed automatically using an existing and experimentally-validated computational chess aesthetics model. The generated chess problems were also assessed by human experts in the domain. The results suggest that attributes collected and recombined from chess and other domains using the DSNS approach can indeed be used to automatically generate chess problems of reasonably high aesthetic quality. In particular, a low quality chess source (i.e. tournament game sequences between weak players) used in combination with actual photographs of people was able to produce three-move chess problems of comparable quality or better to three-move chess problems generated using a high quality chess source (i.e. published compositions by human experts), and more efficiently as well. Why information from a foreign domain can be integrated and functional in this way remains an open question for now. The DSNS approach is, in principle, scalable and applicable to any domain in which objects have attributes that can be represented using real numbers.
syn_none.coling::28a6b262-a893-4fcb-a538-fc9aa5ad:
The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak, seen in the cosmic matter
distribution at redshifts up to ~3.5, reflects the continued expansion of the
sonic horizon first identified in temperature anisotropies of the cosmic
microwave background. The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak position can now be measured to better than
~1% accuracy using galaxies, and ~1.4-1.6% precision with Ly-alpha forrests and
the clustering of quasars. In conjunction with the Alcock-Paczy\'nski (AP)
effect, which arises from the changing ratio of angular to spatial/redshift
size of (presumed) spherically-symmetric source distributions with distance,
the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurement is viewed as one of the most powerful tools to use in
assessing the geometry of the Universe. In this paper, we employ five baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak
measurements from the final release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV, at
average redshifts <z>=0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48 and 2.33, to carry out a direct
head-to-head comparison of the standard model, Lambda-CDM, and one of the standard model's
principal competitors, known as the R_h=ct universe. For completeness, we
complement the Alcock-Paczy\'nski (AP) diagnostic with a volume-averaged distance probe that assumes
a constant comoving distance scale r_d. Both probes are free of uncertain
parameters, such as the Hubble constant, and are therefore ideally suited for
this kind of model selection. We find that R_h=ct is favored by these
measurements over the standard model based solely on the Alcock-Paczy\'nski (AP) effect, with a
likelihood ~75% versus ~25%, while Planck-Lambda-CDM is favored over R_h=ct
based solely on the volume-averaged distance probe, with a likelihood ~80%
versus ~20%. A joint analysis using both probes produces an inconclusive
outcome, yielding comparable likelihoods to both models. We are therefore not
able to confirm with this work that the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data, on the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data's own, support an
accelerating Universe.
syn_none.coling::f4961832-eeb4-41fc-8a64-82c30107: Let me preface this statement by saying that I really do like Cowboy Bebop. The animation and designs are sublime, the soundtrack is fantastic, the action is great, and when all three elements come together Cowboy Bebop can occasionally become a jaw dropping audiovisual masterpiece, particularly in the breathtaking finale. However, there are so many problems with Cowboy Bebop that I cannot in good faith call Cowboy Bebop a "masterpiece" or proclaim Cowboy Bebop to be one of the best of the medium as anything other than a gateway show. I'll start off with the characters, which is where many of my problems lie. I'll admit, Spike and Jet are great characters, but Spike and Jet are only 2 of the 5 of the entire Bebop Crew. Ein's introduction as a "data dog" or otherwise hyperintelligent canine goes nowhere and Ein spends the rest of Cowboy Bebop just being the Bebop Crew's pet. Faye exhibits many of the worst characteristics that can be written about a female character; Faye is bossy, greedy, obsessed with Faye's own beauty, needs to either be rescued or is a hinderance to the Bebop Crew more often than an asset, Faye often wears revealing clothing for the sole purpose of fanservice. Ed is hit or miss, and Ed walks the line between endearing and annoying, but Ed hardly receives much development beyond Ed's introductory episode. The main villain Vicious is especially bad. Vicious has very little character and motivation aside from a desire for more power, and even though Cowboy Bebop goes a bit into Vicious's backstory Cowboy Bebop never establishes motivation. At the end of Cowboy Bebop, Vicious is little more than an evil guy in a black coat with enough fighting skill that Vicious makes Spike struggle to land a bullet in Vicious, aside from the obvious fact that Vicious becomes a representation of the syndicate Spike ran away from. As a result the five episodes that involve Vicious (Sympathy for the Devil, Jupiter Jazz parts 1 and 2, and Real Folk Blues parts 1 and 2) don't leave me feeling as if the five episodes are as spectacular as Cowboy Bebop wants me to feel like the five episodes are. Aside from that problem, the quality of the episodes varies dramatically. For an episodic show that only has about five episodes that build an overall story, that variation is saying a lot. Sure, there are fantastic episodes such as Waltz for Venus and Ganymede Elegy, but there are also fairly ho hum episodes such as Bohemian Rhapsody, Speak Like a Child, and Boogie Woogie Feng Shui. Reddit, help me appreciate Cowboy Bebop and tell me what I'm missing. Hello, users of CMV! This statement is a footnote from your moderators. We'd just like to remind you of a couple of things. syn_none.coling::17ad7e76-2fa1-4c9b-a42b-44a53287: The truth is that I am actually undecided on this issue, but I will start on the side against gay marriage for two reasons: 1. I lean less towards my starting side and the starting side seems much more fragile and unpopular, so advocating for a weaker position I feel less strongly about helps to practice my argument articulation skills. 2. I believe that the burden of proof is on the side in favor of gay marriage (as I will explain), so I started on the other side. First, please watch [this video] (the video is only two minutes). Due to this argument, I feel that the burden of proof is on the people that wish to redefine the criteria for the institution of marriage (I do not have problems with redefinition itself, but I am just saying that redefinition requires compelling reason). When people answer the question "Do you think gay marriage is a good idea?" with "Why not?," this answer is really just the teapot fallacy (attempting to shift the burden of proof). I do not believe equality is a good argument. The truth is that people with different sexual orientation deserve equal rights to life, liberty, freedom, and the pursuit of happiness as detailed by the constitution. However, the whole equality thing is a red herring in this particular instance. Marriage is not a kind of privilege or a right that must be equal for all types of relationships. Marriage is an institution built around procreation, and homosexual relationships, which may be loving and committed, by definition are non-procreational. There are also heterosexual marriages which are non-procreational, such as old couples or infertile couples, but if you watched the video, you'll understand why the old couples or infertile couples are not analogous; just because there are exceptions to the norm, doesn't mean you can extend the definition to a non-norm, as the norms are not defined by the exceptions to the norm. This "equality" is not the same as women voting or black people being free. Many times the criteria is presented as (a posed question): "If two people love each other, why shouldn't two people be able to get married?" Marriage criteria have nothing to do with love, or even romantic love for that matter. If your criteria are two individuals who have romantic love or sexual love, then incest is fair game. Some will argue that incest is different because within the family, there are power issues, and also genetic defects. There can be power issues within any relationship, whether heterosexual relationship, homosexual relationship, or incestuous relationship. There is no reason to base marriage legislation on power issues. Also, incestuous couples don't have to have children, incestuous couples can adopt, or incestuous couples may be infertile couples or homosexual. One may argue that incest should be a valid form of marriage as well as homosexuality. You can try to argue this point if you want, but please include valid reasoning as the burden of proof is on you. The "why would you care?" argument is invalid; Just because a proposition does not affect anyone adversely, doesn't mean we can change institutions at whim. Even under utilitarianism, this argument doesn't work. Gay people can have fulfilling long-term romantic relationships and sexual relationships without calling the romantic relationships and sexual relationships marriage. Redefining marriage for the happiness of a group is akin (logically, not emotionally) to giving in to lobbyist demands so that lobbyists will be happier. Most arguments for gay marriage are appeals to emotion or popularity. The term "gay rights" was designed to make the term sound like we have internment camps for gay people. Even the term "homophobe" was coined to stigmatize the opposition. Just because this issue is popular in our zeitgeist, and many of the opponents are religious fundamentalists who use straw man arguments, doesn't make the "more reasonable side" correct. If there was a movement to legalize incestuous marriage and incestuous marriage was popular, with videos and websites online that glorified the struggle of such couples, most people would be for incestuous marriage as well. Why is one sexual deviation (and I mean to use that term with complete respect and absolutely no stigma, connotation, or implication) more "marriageable" than another sexual deviation? View changed. In all fairness, I was already 75 there when I wrote this.

syn_none.coling::6ea6d618-d59e-455d-a265-490e1418: There are many reasons why a program might crash. Here are some common reasons: Division by zero: A person may remember from kindergarten math that a person can't divide a number by zero. The result is undefined. Well, if a program tells the computer to divide something by zero, the computer will tell the program that the program is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, the program may crash. Access violation: A program is only allowed to access certain parts of memory. Other parts of memory are off-limits. If a program tries to access part of memory that is off-limits, the computer will tell the program that the program is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, the program may crash. Deadlock: Let's say a person and the person's friend Billy are playing with blocks. The person has the red block, and Billy has the blue block. The person wants to switch blocks, so the person tells Billy that the person will give Billy the red block after Billy gives the person the blue block. Billy tells the person that Billy will give the person the blue block after the person gives Billy the red block. Both the person and Billy will sit there forever waiting for the other person to hand over the other person's block, and the person and Billy will never get anything done. That is a deadlock situation, and when a deadlock situation happens inside a program, the program freezes up and there is nothing a person can do except kill the program and start the program again. Unhandled exception: Sometimes a program will have a special sort of error checking built into the program. When an error is detected, part of the program throws an exception, and another part of the program is supposed to catch the exception and deal with the exception. If an exception gets thrown and is not caught by any part of the program, then usually a dialog will pop up letting a person know that a problem was not dealt with properly, and the program will terminate. All of these situations are caused by bugs in the program. Bugs are just parts of the program that are not written correctly, or don't account for every possible thing that can happen. Some programs have more bugs than other programs. Why? Maybe because the people who wrote the program were in more of a rush or didn't test the program as well as the people should have, or because the program is so complicated that the program is difficult to deal with every possible situation that might happen. Think of a program as a way to do things - a common example given is how to make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. A person's first program might read: get bread get peanut butter get jelly get knife put peanut butter on one slice put jelly on other slice put bread together SERVE If a person runs out of peanut butter, the person is stuck halfway through the instructions without anywhere left to go - that's a crash. A more complicated program would describe how a pizza restaurant works - there's more ingredients, more ways to combine the ingredients, a person has a lot of different workers coming and going at the same time a bunch more things that can go wrong. There's things that can go wrong a person can fix things that can't be fixed - things that can't be fixed or people are too lazy to fix are crashes.

syn_none.coling::a9b058a8-5ce8-448f-820a-6ffba640: Because of the camera's field of view (FOV). If you're a big first person shooter game player (or you know about cameras) you're probably familiar with FOV. If we consider what we can see as a cone starting at our eye and expanding out like [this] (URL0) then FOV is the angle between the two boundary lines. In shooter games FOV is often expanded by pros to gain an advantage, since FOV lets you see more of your surroundings. [Here] (URL1) is a quick example of increasing a game's FOV I googled up. The image on the left has the FOV expanded to 65 degrees compared to the default of 45 degrees on the left. With the larger FOV you can see more on the left and right. But you'll also notice that the 2 trailer things look like the 2 trailer things are farther away even though the player is standing in the same place - the 2 trailer things look like the 2 trailer things are farther away because as you increase the FOV you also change how the light from distant objects is going to converge on your 2D surface. Essentially a larger FOV means that objects seem to decrease in size faster as objects get farther away. The opposite is also true, if you decrease the FOV then decreasing the FOV increases the apparent size of far away objects since far away objects now converge on a larger portion of the view area. The camera on DSCOVR used to take these pictures has a FOV of just 0.61deg. The camera makes the camera very effective at collecting light from far away objects because the camera is focused on a very small cone. The camera also means that the distance between the Earth and the Moon doesn't have the same effect on relative size as the distance between the Earth and the Moon does when taken with a regular camera or human eyes.," "Hold your hand in front of your face. Your hand is probably about as big as your monitor. Keep your hand in the same spot and move your head backwards. Your hand now appears smaller than the monitor. There's a certain distance where your hand and the monitor get smaller together, at the same rate. Your hand and the monitor get smaller together at the same rate because the distance between you and your hand and the monitor becomes a lot greater than the distance between your hand and the monitor. Angular diameter depends on distance, and ratio of distances. Basically, the first image is very close to the moon and far from the earth, so the moon seems big. The second image is very far from both the earth and the moon, so the earth and the moon appear like the actual relative sizes of the earth and the moon. So yes, the earth DOES appear smaller in the second image, but the moon got smaller a lot faster just like your hand.," "DSCOVR basically had the camera of DSCOVR zoomed in more. The EPIC camera on the spacecraft that took the image is specifically designed to observe the Earth from a distance, whereas the cameras on the Apollo missions were more general purpose. To be more precise, in a camera the focal length of the lens determines the physical size of the image formed on the sensor. Then the physical size of the sensor determines the field of view, and the pixel resolution of the sensor determines the size of each pixel in the image. With analogue film there are no pixels but the analogue film still has a resolution limit because of the chemistry of the analogue film and there's also a resolution limit imposed by the lens. Finally a large image can simply be cropped, although the DSCOVR image is in fact pretty much the full size of the DSCOVR image.
syn_none.coling::3dd39352-d471-4ab9-bd50-b7345fc1: You can call what you're asking about a 'wealth tax', or 'capital tax'. A wealth tax and a capital tax are taxes not based on income you earned in a year, but some measure of how much you own. Some countries (Italy I believe is a prime example) tax ownership of foreign land. Some countries tax amounts owned by corporations [Canada did this until ~5-10 years ago depending on province]. Some countries strictly tax your wealth above a certain level (Switzerland, as has been mentioned, does this). One form of what you are referring to that does exist in the US is the 'Estate Tax'. The Estate Tax is a tax on the amount of wealth that a person owns, at the time the person dies. The threshold for when the Estate Tax applies has been very volatile over the last 20 years, but the threshold is generally in the multi-millions, and I believe the threshold sits somewhere around $5M. If a wealth tax and a capital tax start to crop up more and more (and I believe a wealth tax and a capital tax will), don't be shocked at the initial 'sticker price'. Theoretically a wealth tax could replace some of the current income tax regime in many countries without creating a strict increased tax burden on the people of the countries. ie: if you owe $10k in income tax this year, but a $2k capital tax is instituted next year, then you are still in the same position as long as your income tax is reduced to $8k. Whether a wealth tax and a capital tax are effective or preferable or not is really a question of economics, not personal finance, so I will not belabour that point. Note: if the money you have saved earns money (interest, or dividends, or maybe rent from a condo you own), then the earnings are typically taxed alongside your wage income. Any 'wealth tax' or 'capital tax' as I've described a wealth tax and a capital tax above would be in addition to income tax on investment earnings.
syn_none.coling::8eb96c1a-6193-4f0f-843b-4b91efbe: You could have both options exercised (and assigned to you) on the same day, but I don't think you could lose money on both options on the same day. The reason is that while exercises are immediate, assignments are processed after the markets close at the end of each day. See http://www.888options.com/help/faq/assignment.jsp for details. So you would get both assignments at the same time, that night. The net effect should be that you don't own any stock (someone would put you the stock, then the stock would be called away) and you don't have the options anymore. You should have incoming cash of $1500 selling the stock to the call exerciser and outgoing cash of $1300 buying from the put exerciser, right? So you would have no more options but $200 more cash in your account in the morning. You bought at 13 and sold at 15. This options position is an agreement to buy at 13 and sell at 15 at someone else's option. The way you lose money is if one of the options isn't exercised while the other option is exercised, i.e. if the stock is below 13 so nobody is going to opt to buy from you at 15, but nobody will sell to you at 13; or above 15 so nobody is going to opt to sell to you at 13, but nobody will buy from you at 15. You make money if neither option is exercised (you keep the premium you sold for) or both options are exercised (you keep the gap between the two options, plus the premium). Having both options exercised is surely rare, since early exercise is rare to begin with, and early exercise tends to happen when options are deep in the money; so you would expect both options to be exercised if both options are deep in the money at some point. Having both options be exercised on the same day ... can't be common, but having both options be exercised on the same day is maybe most likely just before expiration with minimal time value, if the stock moves around quickly so both options are in the money at some point during the day.
syn_none.coling::59aec439-babf-4d21-b03b-4f331a96: The first thing you need to do is look at your terms and conditions of your credit card, or ask your bank, how the bank will apply the payments. As Dilip notes in the answer Dilip provides, in the US, the bank will likely apply the minimum payment to the lower rate balance, and then must apply the rest above the minimum payment to the higher rate balance. In other countries, how the bank will apply the payments will vary by law and custom. Do not assume the bank will pay off the higher balance, or proportionally, without asking. Let's take the following example. You owe $6000. $5000 is at 13.5% (normal purchase rate) and $1000 is at 22% (cash advance rate). If your bank applies payments to both balances proportionally, then a payment of $600 will reduce your purchase balance by $500 and your cash advance balance by $100. The average APR, then, is simply sum of the product of the APR times balance. So here, (.135*5000 + .225*1000)/6000 = 15%. This calculation is called a weighted average. If the bank applies the payment differently - such as to the lower rate first, or some specified part to the lower rate and the rest to the higher rate - then this weighted average will be misleading if you enter this weighted average into a calculator, because your average APR will rise over time as you pay off the purchase balance but don't pay off the cash advance balance, or the average APR may decrease if the opposite happens. The weighted average is probably reasonably close in the circumstance that you describe, even if you have rules applying the balance differently, so long as the rules don't 100% pay down the lower rate - so the weighted average may be the simplest option for you in terms of rough calculations (where the rough calculations are not critical to be correct, just close). One approach using the online calculators that might be better, is to treat these balances like two separate loans or two separate cards. Many calculators exist for multiple balances. Then you can allocate funds differently to the two separate cards. This approach would allow you to see how long you will need until you've paid off the higher balance, for example, although this approach probably won't perfectly match things - unless you find a site that has this specific option available you probably will have to either live with a small error in your calculations or do the math by hand.

syn_none.coling::df393828-70be-448f-bbdb-11367e15: I cannot stress this enough, so I'll just repeat this:  Don't plan your finances around your credit score.  Don't even think about your credit score at all.  Plan a budget and stick to your budget.  Make sure you include short and long term savings in your budget.  Pay your bills on time.  Use credit responsibly.  Do all of these things, and your credit score will take care of your credit score.  Don't try to plan your finances around raising your credit score. On the subject of 0% financing specifically, my rule of thumb is to only ever use 0% financing when I have enough money saved up to buy the thing outright, and even then only if my budget will still balance with the added cost of repaying the loan.  Other people have other rules, including not taking such loans at all, and you should develop a rule that works for you (but you should have a rule).  One rule you shouldn't have is "do whatever will optimize your credit score" because you shouldn't plan your finances around your credit score.   All things considered, I think the most important thing in your situation is to make sure that you don't let the teaser rate tempt you into making purchases you wouldn't otherwise make.  You're not really getting free money; you're just shifting around the time frame for payment, and only within a limited window at that.  Also, be sure to read the fine print in the credit agreement; credit agreements can be filled with gotchas and pitfalls.  In particular, if you don't clear the balance by the end of the introductory rate period, you can sometimes incur interest charges retroactively to the date of purchase.  Make sure you know your terms and conditions cold. It sounds like you're just getting started, so best of luck, and remember that Rome wasn't built in a day.  Patience can be the most effective tool in your personal finance arsenal, and patience will serve you well as you develop your financial habits and knowledge over time. p.s. Don't plan your finances around your credit score.

This paper is an extension of Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, showing CNN representations at FC7 layer are to certain extent equivariant to various classes of transformations and that training with a certain group of transformations makes the representations more equivalent.

Authors performed a large amount of experiments, training over 30 networks with different forms of jitter, which is quite impressive. However authors find a main message of this work is rather difficult to find. Yes, authors measured the properties on a different layer than the Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, however authors find some novel insights other than the known fact that jitter helps to achieve invariance is hard to find. The evaluation seems to be mostly correct, however the paper does not seem to be solving the task advertised in the title of this paper really well.

Major issues are in the experiments with the representation distances:
* The selection of only FC7 layer is a bit controversial - FC7 layer is followed only by a single classification layer (FC8 layer) to the common output - class likelyhoods. Because the FC8 layer is just a linear projection, what the equivalence map does is just to re-project the FC8 weights of the attached network to the FC8 weights of the original network. Probably performing similar experiments but on more layers may be more useful (as the networks are already trained).
* The experiment with representation distance is missing what is the classification error on the testing dataset. The classification error on the testing dataset would answer whether the representations are actually compatible up to linear transformation at all...
* The experiment with K-NN is not clear whether the experiment with K-NN is measured per each test set example? After training the equivalence map? More clear would be to show that networks trained on similar group of jitter transformations are more compatible on the target task.
* The proposed method does not seem to improve equivariance consistently on all tasks. Especially with \lambda_1 and \lambda_2 having such small values, the loss is basically equal to simple data jitter as the loss just adds up the loss of the original image and the loss of the transformed image. Maybe the issue is in the selection of the FC7 layer?

In general, this paper shows some interesting results on the FC7 equivariance, but this paper does not seem to be drawing many interesting new observations out of these experiments. Due to some issues with the equivalence experiments and the finetuning of equivariance, acceptance of this manuscript would not be recommended. However, refining the experiments on already trained networks and restructuring this manuscript into more investigative work may lead to interesting contribution to the field.

There are also few minor issues:
* The new criterion for equivariance mapping helps to gain better results is not experimentally verified.
* The angles on page 1 and the angles on page 5 are missing units (degrees?).
* On page three, "In practice, difficult... ", M_g is not M_g which is maximised/minimised, but the loss over the M_g is maximised/minimised
* Page 4, footnote 2 - if you are just halving the activations, halving the activations is hard to call a dropout as this constant factor can be passed to the following weights or the preceding weights
* Is the network for RVL-CDIP the same architecture as Alexnet architecture?
* On page 7, Figure 3a+3b - in my opinion, turning the diagonal elements to white is really misleading, and probably even incorrect, as the distance between the same representations should be zero (which is also a way how to verify that the experiments are performed correctly).
syn_none.coling::07106895-c293-4117-be28-f7598533:
Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle and am very happy to see the application of the information bottleneck principle to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this paper is the first paper that applies the information bottleneck principle to train deep neural networks (the original papers only presented the information bottleneck concept), but see below for the note of independent work claim.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound is very clear, even for those who are not very familiar with variational inference. Also the explanation of the information bottleneck principle is clear. Experimental results seem to be very promising and demonstrate the potential of the information bottleneck principle.

I found the presentation for the model a bit confusing. In variational inference/information maximisation, p usually denotes the model and q represents the "inference engine". This means the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure. However the presented VIB assumed p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** (and approximated p(x, y) by the empirical distribution), thus here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this case, but this definition of p(y|x) makes the two definitions contradict to each other!

The authors have made an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder and the warm-up training (by tuning beta). However, even when the loss function formula is the same to the variational lowerbound used in variational auto-encoder (in this case beta = 1), the underlying model is different! For example, r(z) in VIB is the variational approximation to p(z) (which means r(z) is not a component in the model), while in variational auto-encoder r(z) is the prior distribution which is actually defined in the modelling procedure. Similarly p(z|x) in VIB is included in the model, while in variational auto-encoder p(z|x) is the approximate posterior and p(z|x) can be independently chosen (e.g. you can use p(x|z) as a deep neural network but p(z|x) as a deep neural network or a Gaussian process).

In summary, I think the presentation for the modelling procedure is unclear. I hope these points would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation makes me uncomfortable as a Bayesian person. In the variational auto-encoder part, the variational auto-encoder part should clearly mention the difference between VIB and variational auto-encoder, and provide some intuitions if the VIB interpretation is preferred.


Typos:
Eq. 9-11: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Fig 2 "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

**claim for independent work**
The authors claimed that the manuscript presented an independent work to Chalk et al. 2016 which is online since May 2016. It seems to me that nowadays deep learning research is very competitive that many people publish the same idea at the same time. So I would trust this claim for independent work and commend the honesty of the authors, but in case this claim for independent work is not true, I would not recommend the manuscript for acceptance.
syn_none.coling::745b25d5-34c6-4c43-a690-6414f205:
The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier. Comparison to prior work using continuous or n-gram based language models is well done, even though the paper does not make clear whether the paper also compared against bilingual data selection (e.g. sum of difference of cross-entropies).

The motivation to use a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM was first unclear, but the paper shows strength in arguing that certain sections of a text/sentence are more important than other sections and this importance is achieved by a CNN. However, the paper does not experimentally show whether a BOW representation or SEQ representation (or the combination of BOW representation and SEQ representation) is more important and why BOW representation or SEQ representation is more important.

The textual description of the CNN (one-hot or semi-supervised using pre-trained embeddings) is clear, detailed, and points out the important aspects of the CNN. However, a picture of the layers of the CNN showing how inputs are combined would be worth a thousand words.

The paper is overall well written, but some parentheses for citations are not necessary (\citet vs. \citep) (e.g line 385 of the paper).

Experiments and evaluation support the claims of the paper, but concern exists about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences (line 443 of the paper) based on a separate validation set:

- What validation data is used for the validation set? The paper does not make clear on what data hyperparameters of the CNN models are chosen. How sensitive are the CNN models to hyperparameters?

- Table 2 of the paper should really compare scores of different approaches with the same number of sentences selected. As Figure 1 of the paper shows, the approach of the paper still seems to outperform the baselines in this case.

Other comments:

- Interest exists in an experiment that compares the technique of the paper against baselines when more in-domain data is available, not just the development set.

- The results section or discussion section of the paper could feature some example sentences selected by the different methods to support the claims made in section 5.4 of the paper.

- In regards to the argument of abstracting away from surface forms in section 5.4 of the paper: Another baseline to compare against could have been the work of Axelrod, 2015, who replaces some words with POS tags to reduce LM data sparsity to see whether the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over POS tags.

- Using the sum of source classification scores and target classification scores is very similar to source & target Lewis-Moore LM data selection: sum of difference of cross-entropies. A reference to Lewis-Moore LM data selection around line 435 of the paper would be reasonable.

Finally, wondering exists if weights for the sum of source classification scores and target classification scores could be learned by extending the CNN model to the bilingual setting or parallel setting.
syn_none.coling::4e7728dc-010d-47cb-95f2-16525a71:
In this submission, an interesting approach to character-based language modeling is pursued that retains word-level representations both in the context, and optionally also in the output. However, the approach is not new, cf. (Kim et al. 2015) as cited in the submission, as well as (Jozefowicz et al. 2016). Both Kim and Jozefowicz already go beyond this submission by applying the approach using RNNs/LSTMs. Also, Jozefowicz et al. provide a comparative discussion of different approaches to character-level modeling, which I am missing here, at least by discussing this existing work. The remaining novelty of the approach then would be the application of the approach to machine translation, although the application of the approach remains somewhat unclear, inhowfar reranking of N-best lists can handle the OOV problem - the translation-related part of the OOV problem should be elaborated here. That said, some of the claims of this submission seems somewhat exaggerated, like the statement in Sec. 2.3: "making the notion of vocabulary obsolete", whereas the authors e.g. express doubts concerning the interpretation of perplexity w/o an explicit output vocabulary. For example modeling of especially frequent word forms still can be expected to contribute, as shown in e.g. arXiv:1609.08144
Sec. 2.3: You claim that the objective requires a finite vocabulary. This statement only is correct if the units considered are limited to full word forms. However, using subwords and even individual characters, implicitly larger and even infinite vocabularies can be covered with the log-likelihood criterion. Even though this require a model different from the model proposed here, the corresponding statement should qualified in this respect.
The way character embeddings are used for the output should be clarified. The description in Sec. 2.4 is not explicit enough in my view.
Concerning the configuration of NCE, the configuration of NCE would be desirable to get a better idea of how you arrived at your specific configuration and parameterization described in Sec. 3.4.
Sec. 4.1: you might want to mention that (Kim et al. 2015) came to similar conclusions w.r.t. the performance of using character embeddings at the output, and discuss the suggestions for possible improvements given therein.
Sec. 4.2: there are ways to calculate and interpret perplexity for unknown words, cf. (Shaik et al. IWSLT 2013).
Sec. 4.4 and Table 4: the size of the full training vocabulary should be provided here.
Minor comments:
p. 2, bottom: three different input layer -> three different input layers (plural)
Fig. 1: fonts within Fig. 1 are way too small
p. 3, first item below Fig. 1: that we will note WE -> that we will denote WE
Sec. 2.3: the parameters estimation -> the parameter estimation (or: the parameters' estimation)
p. 5, first paragraph: in factored way -> in a factored way
p. 5, second paragraph: a n-best list, a nk-best list -> an n-best list, an nk-best list
Sec. 4.2, last sentence: Despite adaptive gradient, -> verb and article missing

The paper introduces Edward, a probabilistic programming language
built over TensorFlow and Python, and supporting a broad range of most
popular contemporary methods in probabilistic machine learning.
Quality:
The Edward library provides an extremely impressive collection of
modern probabilistic inference methods in an easily usable form.
The paper provides a brief review of the most important techniques
especially from a representation learning perspective, combined with
two experiments on implementing various modern variational inference
methods and GPU-accelerated HMC.
The first experiment (variational inference) would be more valuable if
the first experiment had a clear link to complete code to reproduce the results
provided. The HMC experiment looks OK, except the characterising Stan
as a hand-optimised implementation seems unfair as the code is clearly
not hand-optimised for this specific model and hardware configuration.
I do not think anyone doubts the quality of the Edward implementation, so
please do not ruin the picture by unsubstantiated sensationalist
claims. Instead of current drama, I would suggest comparing
head-to-head against Stan on single core and separately reporting the
extra speedups Edward gains from parallelisation and GPU. These numbers
would also help the readers to estimate the performance of the method
for other hardware configurations.
Clarity:
The paper is in general clearly written and easy to read. The numerous
code examples are helpful, but also difficult as the code examples are sometimes
unclear what is missing. The code examples would be very helpful if the authors could
provide and clearly link to a machine-readable companion (a Jupyter
notebook would be great, but even text or HTML would be easier to
copy-paste from than a pdf like the paper) with complete runnable code
for all the code examples.
Originality:
The Edward library is clearly a unique collection of probabilistic
inference methods. In terms of the paper, the main threat to novelty
comes from previous publications of the same group. The main paper

Solar power is a miracle of modern science. Solar power has one, tiny little problem, however. Solar power is still more expensive than using other forms of power. If solar power wasn't for the cost, solar power would be a much better idea, but then that goes for all forms of renewable energy.

Many people will point out that installing solar power is on par with or even cheaper than building new power plants, like nuclear power plants or coal power plants. While installing solar power is true in the very large scale, you're probably not going to build your own power plant, and therefore don't have that expense to contend with.

Look at the cost of a solar panel vs. how much power *on average* a solar panel can produce. Do the math.

> I believe if the government invested some money the government could easily shut down one or two nuclear power plants

You seem to be laboring under some false assumptions. Firstly, the government is subsidizing solar power purchases in California in a huge way - so the government *is* investing some money. Secondly, the government does not operate the Nuclear Power Plants - Nuclear Power Plants are operated by private corporations. Nuclear Power Plants are *regulated* by the government. Also, the primary cost of a nuclear power plant is the construction of the nuclear power plant and the disposal of the nuclear material - not the running of the nuclear power plant itself. Shutting down a working nuclear power plant would waste money, not save money.

Like I said, I love solar power, for all kinds of reasons. Solar power is "point of use" which means there is very little loss due to long distance transmission. Solar power is practically zero emissions. Solar power is silent (that's a big thing for me). Solar power provides the greatest benefit when the need is the highest, in the summer, in the daytime.

Possibly the best use of solar power might be to run air conditioning. During the summer when the sun is strong, the need for air conditioning is strong. Use the light provided by solar panels to help cool the building. Also, if the solar panels are on the roof, the solar panels provide shade for the building. Win/win.

Still, on a pure cost / benefit analysis, however, solar power is still cheaper to use coal or natural gas to provide electricity.

Say you're a merchant living in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a bunch of super-rich ladies who really, really loves cumin (as in, the spice). Unfortunately, cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam, a merchant has to go to the middle east or India to get some of that fine cumin so cumin is *super-expensive*. Over there, however, cumin grows like a weed and cumin costs very little money. If only a merchant could get some of that cheap cumin over to Amsterdam, a merchant could make a lot of money!

Unfortunately, the only way to do that is to send out a big-ass ship for like nine months. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (a merchant has to get a ship, and a captain and crew who all wants nine months worth of pay), but sending out a big-ass ship is also really risky. The ship could sink, after all, or all the cumin could spoil.

So how does a merchant accomplish this? Assuming a merchant is not stupendously rich (and very few people or groups, aside from maybe whole nations, are that rich), how does a merchant finance this? A merchant could go to a bank or money-lender and take out a loan, a loan which would have a very steep interest rate that could almost eat up all of the profits. And what if the ship sank? A merchant would be completely bankrupt, and be thrown into prison, if the money-lender doesn't waste the broke ass of the merchant first.

So, a merchant comes up with an idea. A merchant can't finance this trip alone. But a merchant could rather easily finance, say, one tenth of the cost of the trip. And look at that, a merchant has nine friends, all of whom could also afford one tenth of the cost of the trip. So a merchant and nine friends all come to an agreement: a merchant and nine friends decide to each finance part of the cost for the trip (i.e. a merchant and nine friends "buy stock" in the enterprise), each getting shares worth one tenth of the total enterprise. With this money, a merchant and nine friends pay for the ship and crew, send the ship and crew off, and then nine months later, the ship comes back with a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive cumin. The profits far and away compensate for the initial cost, and each of a merchant and nine friends gets one tenth of the enormous profits.

But what happens if the ship sinks? Well, sinking is a real bummer obviously (especially for the crew!), but a merchant only payed for one tenth of the cost, and this was a cost a merchant could afford to eat, a merchant is not gonna get killed over one tenth of the cost. Since the risk was spread around to 10 people, no one landed in debtors prison. Everyone took a small hit, instead of one person taking an enormous hit.

Think about this example, and all the people involved in this example. The fancy ladies got cumin (and for cheaper than the fancy ladies would have otherwise). The shipwrights got work building a new ship. The captain and crew all got work and a salary. The trader in India got a new customer for cumin. And obviously, a merchant and nine friends got really rich in the process. In short, *every single person is better off*, and better off wouldn't have happened if this notion of "buying and selling stocks" didn't exist.

This is the advantage of a stock market. A stock market moves capital around from where capital just lies around doing absolutely nothing to where capital can be put to use, and in the meantime, everybody gets richer. A stock market also distributes risk between lots of people, so a merchant doesn't have to be afraid of going broke all the time.

Now, obviously, there are problems with how the modern day American version of the stock market functions. But the critique is that the stock market stopped doing what the stock market is supposed to be doing (i.e. allocating capital so that capital can be put into productive use) and the stock market stopped being a means to an end, and the stock market became an end unto the stock market. The basic concept of a stock market is a fantastic idea, and a person would have to be a real hard-core communist to oppose a stock market. A stock market is why we have railroads, cars, computers, telephones, cheap and plentiful food, medicine, and all the other modern things we value so highly.

Depends on if your business is a sole proprietorship, single member LLC, multi member LLC, an LLC with the "S" tax election, an S Corporation, or a C Corporation.

Sole Proprietorship: All profits and losses pass to you individually. You're also personally liable for anything that goes wrong. Pro Tip: form an LLC or go get a free consultation with a business attorney.

Single Member LLC: Profits and losses pass through to you personally, but your liability is limited to the LLC's assets. You also have to pay self employment tax.

Multi-Member LLC: Profits and losses are split in proportion to each members ownership interest in the LLC. You also pay self employment tax.

LLC with "S" election: You pay yourself a reasonable salary, and that salary is not subject to the self employment tax. Remaining profits and losses are passed through to you and any other shareholders in proportion to each shareholders percentage interest in the LLC. Whether or not you get taxed on any distributions depends on your basis, but this is where is gets complicated and I can't ELI5 (just let the CPA worry about this)

S Corporation: see above

C Corporation: The C Corporation profits are taxed at the C Corporation tax level and then any dividends made to shareholders are taxed as well. This is called double taxation and double taxation is why C Corporation structures are not ideal for small business owners.

It's about anonymity and vulnerability.

On the internet, you're anonymous and well outside the reach of the person you're talking to, so when people disagree, people tend to be a lot more confrontational and aggressive... because it's easy to be aggressive and confrontational when there's no chance of being punched in the face.

In the real world if you're 5" tall and weigh 90lbs soaking wet, you're probably not going to tell a 6"5 250lb guy that the guy is full of shit, even if that's what you think. Online, who cares? What's the guy going to do?

The flip side is it's also much easier to be abusive or aggressive (or honest) when the person you're communicating with is just words on a screen. The internet dehumanizes the person you're speaking to.

Basically, it's really easy to watch a bad youtube video and tell xXUsernameXx that xXUsernameXx is a talentless piece of shit. It's a different thing to watch that same video and then walk up to Jenny, the 14 year old girl who makes Minecraft videos to take Jenny's mind off Jenny's parent's divorce...and look Jenny in the eye and say "You're a talentless piece of shit."

As for cars? Well, the same applies. You're in a big, locked metal box that's basically half suit of armor, half escape pod. Lean on your horn, give the middle finger, because you're at your turning and will never see whoever's driving that car again.. and fuck that fucking stupid fucking Ford that cut you off in traffic, because that Ford is a stupid fucking Ford...not Jenny's Mom who's had a really bad day and distracted because Jenny's Mom doesn't know how Jenny's Mom is going to make rent that week. The energy of the clap remains unchanged so we look at where that energy is going. In a regular clap on earth, the energy of the collision goes into a variety of things;

1) sound

2) deformation of your hands

3) heat

4) some others that are probably constant in both scenarios and I won't address

Let's model (horribly roughly) a clap. 2 hands, each at 500g moving at 2m/s. E=mv2 so E= 4J roughly.

Even though a clap would be considered an ellastic collision there is likely some small energy loss to deformation. I would expect to see some damage to cells under a microscope but very little. The biggest consumer of energy is going to be the heat given off. From [here](_URL_0_) we see a clap is about 20ms long (super rough) and from [here](_URL_1_) we can see the sound power of a few similar things, let's say an alarm clock is close enough. Even if we're wrong by a factor of a 100x, the factor is still close enough for this discussion. By doing the roughest, dirtiest integration of the sound wave shown in the first link with the power output of the table in the second link, we get a total energy of 2x10^-6 J of energy from a clap. Compared the the 4J of input energy into the collision, in earth, the sound energy is only 0.00005% of the total energy released. The rest of the energy goes to heat and deformation, and I wouldn't even bother guessing at what the ratio is between heat and deformation.

So, to answer your question:

On earth, only 0.00005% of the energy goes into the sound of a clap. The rest of the energy goes into heat and deformation of your hands. In space, 0% of the energy goes into sound and that tiny bit of energy that would have gone into sound on earth simply goes into more heat. The energy of the sound of the clap is so low by comparison to the heat given off by the collision to start with that the collision is essentially unchanged except you hear no sound.
syn_none.coling::8e0f7cff-07ca-48c6-b381-34b577d1: Before babies start to use language babies form speech through babble. Basically babies play with producing noise through open mouths and closed mouths. These utterances are the easiest utterances for developmental babies to make as babies explore sounds. Think of the open mouths and closed mouths like binary code: 0 = the open vowel sound, like 'aaaaaa'. Then 1 (or in binary code a closed mouth) = the closed consonant sound, like 'm' or 'p'. Try the closed consonant sound. Close your mouth as if you were making the beginning of a 'm' word or 'p' word, then just open your mouth and push through some air.... You're basically making the 'ma' sound and 'pa' sound. 'B', 'D', and 'P' are pretty much interchangeable as closed consonants. Hence the variations found: baba, abba, papa, dada, etc. So, these utterances are the basic building blocks of vocalisation, so these utterances are the utterances babies use. The simplest form for the human mouth. Another interesting question is that these pre-linguistic babies have been the babies to give birth to language in the naming of mother and father. Why did people follow the lead of babies? Maybe the simple naming of 'poo' and 'wee' in many languages follow a similar explanation. Grandparents also have similar binary forms in many languages too, like in Hindi. Paternal Grandfather — दादा (daadaa) Paternal Grandmother — दादी (daadii) Maternal Grandfather — नाना (naanaa) Maternal Grandmother — नानी (naanii). These naming patterns in Hindi show how the binary forms that babies discover become the foundation for naming family members across different languages and cultures, demonstrating the universal nature of these basic vocalisation building blocks that babies naturally produce.

syn_none.coling::f249dac3-f3a2-4db9-9758-e18c9f8f: There are a bunch of people in a town. The people all live in apartment, and some of the people are looking to move to houses. The house-builders in this town see this demand and start building houses. When the house-builders look for people to buy these houses, there is a lot of demand, so this demand can push prices higher as there is more competition for supply. (the opposite of competition on the supply-side, where competition brings prices down) A bunch of people buy houses at these high-demand prices, and prices continue to climb as demand remains high. But, once the price gets too high, or most of the demand subsides from everyone wanting a house having a house, there suddenly becomes much lower demand, dropping the cost of purchasing a house. Those people that have already purchased a house now are seeing the people as losing money, and the people want to move back into an apartment while getting rid of the house; this demand cranks up supply, causing a precipitous drop on prices for these houses. The drop continues until the prices reach a level that demand begins to stabilize at a new level. --- When we talk about a bubble, a bubble really comes down to a market of low-supply, high-demand quickly changing to a high-supply, low-demand market. The major problem is that both versions help the versions: high-demand brings people in to invest and take advantage of the price increases, while low-demand gets people to try to push away from the market, making supply even higher. This high-demand and low-demand pattern creates instability in prices and supply relationships that characterize bubble behavior in markets for houses and other goods.

syn_none.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) is a key cybersecurity tool for network administrators as An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) identifies malicious traffic and cyberattacks. With the recent successes of machine learning techniques such as deep learning, more and more Intrusion Detection Systems are now using machine learning algorithms to detect attacks faster. However, these Intrusion Detection Systems lack robustness when facing previously unseen types of attacks. With the increasing number of new attacks, especially against Internet of Things devices, having a robust Intrusion Detection System able to spot unusual and new attacks becomes necessary. This work explores the possibility of leveraging generative adversarial models to improve the robustness of machine learning based Intrusion Detection Systems. More specifically, this work proposes a new method named SIGMA, that leverages adversarial examples to strengthen Intrusion Detection Systems against new types of attacks. Using Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and metaheuristics, SIGMA generates adversarial examples, iteratively, and uses adversarial examples to retrain a machine learning-based Intrusion Detection System, until a convergence of the detection rate (i.e. until the detection system is not improving anymore). A round of improvement consists of a generative phase, in which SIGMA uses Generative Adversarial Networks and metaheuristics to generate instances; an evaluation phase in which SIGMA calculates the detection rate of those newly generated attacks; and a training phase, in which SIGMA trains the Intrusion Detection System with those attacks. SIGMA method has been evaluated for four standard machine learning classification algorithms acting as Intrusion Detection Systems, with a combination of Generative Adversarial Networks and a hybrid local-search and genetic algorithm, to generate new datasets of attacks. The results show that SIGMA can successfully generate adversarial attacks against different machine learning based Intrusion Detection Systems. Also, using SIGMA, SIGMA can improve the performance of an Intrusion Detection System to up to 100 after as little as two rounds of improvement.
syn_none.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Phylogenetic networks are leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs that are used to describe non-treelike evolutionary histories and are thus a generalization of phylogenetic trees. The hybridization number of a phylogenetic network is the sum of all indegrees minus the number of nodes plus one. The Hybridization Number problem takes as input a collection of phylogenetic trees and asks to construct a phylogenetic network that contains an embedding of each of the input phylogenetic trees and has a smallest possible hybridization number. We present an algorithm for the Hybridization Number problem on three binary phylogenetic trees on n leaves, which runs in time O ( c k poly (n, with k the hybridization number of an optimal phylogenetic network and c some positive constant. For the case of two phylogenetic trees, an algorithm with running time O ( 3.18 k n) was proposed before whereas an algorithm with running time O ( c k poly (n for more than two phylogenetic trees had prior to this article remained elusive. The algorithm for two phylogenetic trees uses the close connection to acyclic agreement forests to achieve a linear exponent in the running time, while previous algorithms for more than two phylogenetic trees (explicitly or implicitly) relied on a brute force search through all possible underlying phylogenetic network topologies, leading to running times that are not O ( c k poly (n, for any c . The connection to acyclic agreement forests is much weaker for more than two phylogenetic trees, so even given the right acyclic agreement forest, the reconstruction of the phylogenetic network poses major challenges. We prove novel structural results that allow us to reconstruct a phylogenetic network without having to guess the underlying topology. The techniques of us generalize to more than three input phylogenetic trees with the exception of one key lemma that maps nodes in the phylogenetic network to phylogenetic tree nodes and, thus, minimizes the amount of guessing involved in constructing the phylogenetic network. The main open problem therefore is to prove results that establish such a mapping for more than three phylogenetic trees.
syn_none.coling::0c653e8b-8157-47f3-bdaa-142023fb: We introduce the binary value principle which is a simple subset-sum instance expressing that a natural number written in binary cannot be negative, relating the binary value principle to central problems in proof and algebraic complexity. We prove conditional superpolynomial lower bounds on the Ideal Proof System (IPS) refutation size of the binary value principle, based on a well-known hypothesis by Shub and Smale about the hardness of computing factorials, where IPS is the strong algebraic proof system introduced by Grochow and Pitassi. Conversely, we show that short IPS refutations of the binary value principle bridge the gap between sufficiently strong algebraic proof systems and semi-algebraic proof systems. Our results extend to full-fledged IPS the paradigm introduced in Forbes et al., whereby lower bounds against subsystems of IPS were obtained using restricted algebraic circuit lower bounds, and demonstrate that the binary value principle captures the advantage of semi-algebraic reasoning over algebraic reasoning, for sufficiently strong algebraic proof systems and sufficiently strong semi-algebraic proof systems. Specifically, we show the following: Conditional IPS lower bounds: item Conditional IPS lower bounds: The Shub-Smale hypothesis implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of the binary value principle over the rationals defined as the unsatisfiable linear equation i 1 n 2 - i 1 x i - 1, for boolean x i 's. Further, the related -conjecture implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of a variant of the binary value principle over the ring of rational functions. No prior conditional lower bounds were known for IPS or for apparently much weaker propositional proof systems such as Frege. 1 1 footnote 1 Though simple, the binary value principle is not a direct translation of a boolean formula, hence, similar to and other results on algebraic proofs (e.g., Razborov), IPS lower bounds on the binary value principle do not necessarily entail lower bounds for Frege or subsystems of Frege. Algebraic proof systems vs. semi-algebraic proof systems: item Algebraic proof systems vs. semi-algebraic proof systems: Admitting short refutations of the binary value principle is necessary for any algebraic proof system to fully simulate any known semi-algebraic proof system, and for strong enough algebraic proof systems admitting short refutations of the binary value principle is also sufficient. In particular, we introduce a very strong proof system that simulates all known semi-algebraic proof systems (and most other known concrete propositional proof systems), under the name Cone Proof System (CPS), as a semi-algebraic analogue of the ideal proof system: CPS establishes the unsatisfiability of collections of polynomial equalities and inequalities over the reals, by representing sum-of-squares proofs (and extensions) as algebraic circuits. We prove that IPS is polynomially equivalent to CPS iff IPS admits polynomial-size refutations of the binary value principle (for the language of systems of equations that have no 01-solutions), over both Z and Q.
syn_none.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians and graph-Laplacian spectral embeddings play an important role in multiple areas of machine learning. This paper is focused on graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for the spectral clustering of data as a primary application, however, graph-Laplacian dimension reduction can also be applied in data mining, data manifold learning, etc. Spectral embedding provides a low-dimensional parametrization of the data manifold which makes the subsequent task (e.g., clustering with k-means or any of the k-means approximations) much easier. However, despite reducing the dimensionality of data, the overall computational cost may still be prohibitive for large data sets due to two factors. First, computing the partial eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically requires a large Krylov subspace. Second, after the spectral embedding is complete, one still has to operate with the same number of data points, which may ruin the efficiency of the approach. For example, clustering of the embedded data is typically performed with various relaxations of k-means which computational cost scales poorly with respect to the size of data set. Also, k-means relaxations become prone to getting stuck in local minima, so k-means relaxations robustness depends on the choice of initial guess. In this work, we switch the focus from the entire data set to a subset of graph vertices (target subset). We develop two novel algorithms for such low-dimensional representation of the original graph that preserves important global distances between the nodes of the target subset. In particular, low-dimensional representation allows to ensure that target subset clustering is consistent with the spectral clustering of the full data set if one would perform spectral clustering of the full data set. That is achieved by a properly parametrized reduced-order model (ROM) of the graph-Laplacian that approximates accurately the diffusion transfer function of the original graph for inputs and outputs restricted to the target subset. Working with a small target subset reduces greatly the required dimension of Krylov subspace and allows to exploit the conventional algorithms (like k-means approximations) in the regimes when conventional algorithms are most robust and efficient. This was verified in the numerical clustering experiments with both synthetic data and real data. We also note that our ROM approach can be applied in a purely transfer-function-data-driven way, so ROM approach becomes the only feasible option for extremely large graphs that are not directly accessible. There are several uses for our algorithms. First, our algorithms can be employed on our algorithms own for representative subset clustering in cases when handling the full graph is either infeasible or simply not required. Second, our algorithms may be used for quality control. Third, as our algorithms drastically reduce the problem size, our algorithms enable the application of more sophisticated algorithms for the task under consideration (like more powerful k-means approximations based on semi-definite programming (SDP) instead of the conventional Lloyd's algorithm). Finally, our algorithms can be used as building blocks of a multi-level divide-and-conquer type algorithm to handle the full graph. The multi-level divide-and-conquer type algorithm will be reported in a separate article.
syn_none.coling::d9b96a87-ee9b-46e9-995f-edfccd85: We consider the problem of designing [ n , k ] linear codes for distributed storage systems (DSS) that satisfy the (r , t) - Local Repair Property , where any t ( t) simultaneously failed nodes can be locally repaired, each failed node with locality r . The parameters n , k , r , t are positive integers such that r k n and t - n k . We consider the functional repair model and the sequential approach for repairing multiple failed nodes. By functional repair, we mean that the packet stored in each newcomer is not necessarily an exact copy of the lost data but a symbol that keep the (r , t) -local repair property. By the sequential approach, we mean that the t newcomers are ordered in a proper sequence such that each newcomer can be repaired from the live nodes and the newcomers that are ordered before each newcomer.
