syn_max.coling::9600c031-1ba2-4882-9aa0-8cb6b07d: Operation Claw () constituted a joint Swedish–American undertaking, receiving Norwegian assistance, that unfolded at Lillehammer shortly following the German surrender by World War II's conclusion. Thirty-five Wehrmacht intelligence specialists were relocated along with various equipment initially to Sweden and subsequently to U.S. detention facilities in occupied Germany through an arrangement between the Americans and the German High Command of military forces in Norway. Intelligence material from this undertaking, among it a Soviet codebook, became extremely useful for the United States during the Cold War period. This endeavor proved controversial both when it occurred and afterwards. In 1945, controversy arose because the United States operated in what was perceived as a British controlled nation, and because they secured information about their ally the Soviet Union, in cooperation with neutral Sweden. In later decades, a hypothesis that the Norwegian resistance fighter Kai Holst's sudden death in June 1945 was connected to his involvement in this undertaking has been put forward by among others the historian Tore Pryser. Even before the European conflict ended the various allied states had begun searching for German scientists and other Wehrmacht expertise. Signals intelligence had been vital during World War II and especially the British work with breaking Wehrmacht codes, from the Enigma cipher had been of huge importance. The Yalta Conference in February 1945 had revealed conflicts of interest between the western allied nations on one side and the Soviet Union and relations were severely strained. American intelligence organizations were very interested in Wehrmacht intelligence experts' knowledge of the Soviet Union and immediately after the European conflict ended they began cooperating with the Wehrmacht Major General Reinhard Gehlen and his organization Fremde Heere Ost (FHO) which had led Wehrmacht intelligence on the Eastern Front. It constituted part of an organized effort to obtain as much Wehrmacht intelligence information and personnel as possible; this endeavor had the name Target Intelligence Committee (TICOM). However, fighting continued in East-Asia, the US and the Soviet Union remained allies and Washington was counting on Soviet assistance in combat against Japan. The allies had designated Norway as part of Britain's sphere of influence. Both for Washington and neutral Sweden this endeavor was thus extremely sensitive and was conducted in great secrecy. In the Wehrmacht camp at Lillehammer a group of thirty-five Wehrmacht experts on signals intelligence were gathered. They had been working on the Eastern Front against Soviet forces and possessed an archive and extensive knowledge about Soviet affairs. This constituted knowledge the Western Allies, and especially Washington, wanted and that probably also proved useful during subsequent Cold War tensions. In cooperation with the American intelligence organization Office of Strategic Services (OSS) and with knowledge and assistance from the Norwegian legation in Stockholm agents for the Swedish intelligence organization C-byrån traveled together with two Norwegian intelligence specialists to Lillehammer on May ninth and tenth, 1945. The Wehrmacht group of experts were taken out of detention and transported to Sweden. After a few weeks in Sweden they were on June twelfth flown from Torslanda Airport close to Gothenburg to US occupied Germany and were interned in an American military detention facility at Wiesbaden. The transfer to Sweden of the Wehrmacht experts at Lillehammer, that OSS called this endeavor, was directed from the highest level. From the U.S. side the leader of OSS, Major General William J. Donovan was involved, from the Swedish side the chief of the Defense Staff, Major General Carl August Ehrensvärd. The famous Swedish police director Harry Söderman was also involved from Stockholm's side. More than a month after Wehrmacht capitulation, a British led search supported by Norwegian personnel was executed in order to find people from Gestapo and other Wehrmacht key personnel that tried to hide among ordinary soldiers in Wehrmacht military camps. The search force that Kai Holst and other Norwegians were assisting were soon aware of that a number of Wehrmacht key personnel had been removed in the Swedish–American endeavor a month earlier. Kai Holst had been working at the military office number four (Mi4) at the Norwegian legation in Stockholm, and after the search he unexpectedly traveled right back to Stockholm. The next day he was found shot at the top of the staircase in an apartment building at Rindögatan forty-two on Gärdet. The official cause of death was stated as suicide, but neither Holst's family nor many of his colleagues from the resistance movement have accepted this and are of the opinion that he was liquidated. The historian Tore Pryser has put forward the hypothesis that Holst brought with him documentation from Lillehammer that could damage this undertaking and thus was killed. To be able to damage this endeavor Kai Holst cannot have been trusted as others were. He must have been considered a threat due to his contact with Alexandra Kollontaj who was ambassador in Stockholm representing the Soviet Union. A possible reason for a murder of Kai Holst was thus not his knowledge as such but his connections. This undertaking was the beginning of the postwar era cooperation between Swedish and US intelligence services, in violation of Stockholm's officially stated neutrality. From Washington's perspective this endeavor was viewed as a great success and the responsible within OSS, William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman, were both honored with decorations where this undertaking specifically were mentioned. For the Swedish C-byrån this endeavor quickly became toxic. Even though this undertaking was to be kept confidential, details leaked to the Swedish press and C-byrån were dissolved in February 1946. Details regarding this undertaking continued to be classified as confidential in the post-conflict years and some of it still remains so today. A report about this endeavor in the British National Archives is restricted until 2020.

Honeymoon Hotel is a 1934 Warner Bros. Merrie Melodies cartoon directed by Earl Duvall. The short was released on February 17, 1934.

This production was supervised by Earl Duvall. Character animation came from Jack King, Frank Tipper, both credited, Bob Clampett, Paul Fennell, Chuck Jones and Frank Tashlin, final four uncredited. Musical scoring was composed by Bernard Brown (solely credited) and Norman Spencer (solely uncredited). Audio recording was handled solely by Bernard Brown in an uncredited capacity. Production number 6125.

Plot
This animated work follows a male and female bug/insect who check into a lodging establishment which catches on fire.

Music
The song "Honeymoon Hotel" (by Al Dubin and Harry Warren) was originally introduced in the 1933 Warner Bros. picture Footlight Parade. This brief theatrical piece appears on the DVD release of that motion picture.

Color process
This movie is notable for being the first Warner Bros. cartoon produced in color. It used Cinecolor since Walt Disney had exclusive rights to the Technicolor process. There was only one other Merrie Melodies cartoon produced in Cinecolor (Beauty and the Beast) before the series went briefly back to black-and-white. Later, the Merrie Melodies moved to Technicolor, though the Looney Tunes continued to be produced in black-and-white until 1943. Cinecolor would make a return in several late 1940s Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies shorts.

Contemporary Hellenic visual creativity encompasses works produced during the interval stretching from the establishment of the newly autonomous nation through the conclusion of the nineteenth century.

Since continental territories remained under Ottoman dominion throughout four complete centuries, these regions never participated in the Renaissance nor subsequent aesthetic developments sweeping across Western Europe. Nevertheless, Hellenic islands including Crete, plus the Ionian archipelago specifically, experienced extended intervals under Venetian or alternative European powers' control, thereby gaining superior capacity to absorb the revolutionary aesthetic transformations occurring throughout Europe between the fourteenth and eighteenth centuries.

The Cretan movement plus particularly the Heptanese tradition represent two significant aesthetic developments within Greece that pursued parallel trajectories alongside Western Europe.

Contemporary Hellenic visual creativity can be understood as having been chiefly molded by the distinctive socioeconomic circumstances of the nation, the substantial diaspora population scattered throughout Europe, plus the emerging social elite, alongside external aesthetic influences emanating predominantly from Germany and France.

Three-dimensional works and two-dimensional imagery

Nineteenth century

The Bavarian Academy

Contemporary Hellenic visual production commenced development approximately during the Romanticism era. National creators absorbed numerous components from their European counterparts, yielding the culmination of a distinctive manner of Hellenic Romantic expression, inspired by revolutionary ideals plus the nation's geography and historical legacy. Following centuries of Ottoman dominion, scarce opportunities for education in visual disciplines existed within the recently liberated nation, making foreign study imperative for aspiring creators. Munich, functioning as a crucial international hub for aesthetic disciplines during that era, became the destination where the majority of nineteenth-century Hellenic creators elected to pursue training. Within the Bavarian academy, directed by Karl von Piloty, authentic fresco techniques were taught for mural execution on fresh wet lime plaster. Throughout this interval much creative output displayed emotional and theatrical qualities. The most prominent subjects of the Bavarian academy included urban existence, countryside living, inanimate objects, plus natural scenery.

Subsequently, they would return home and transmit their acquired knowledge. Some remained in Munich, the so-called Athens on the Isar. Both scholarly and personal connections evolved between early Hellenic creators and Bavarian artistry, giving birth to the Hellenic "Bavarian Academy" tradition. Nikolaos Gysis served as an influential instructor and creator at the Bavarian Academy, soon becoming a prominent figure among national creators. Academism, realism, genre depiction, upper middle class portraiture, inanimate object representation and natural scenery depiction, frequently displaying impressionist characteristics, would be superseded near the close of the nineteenth century by Symbolism, Jugendstil, and Art Nouveau, primarily evident in the output of Nikolaos Gysis, Aristeas plus others. Early-twentieth-century modernism is likewise represented by significant Hellenic creators in Munich. Numerous Bavarian Academy creators selected subjects including everyday national existence, local customs, plus living circumstances. Several important practitioners emerged during this interval. Theodoros Vryzakis specialized in historical depiction, especially inspired by the 1821 Independence War. Nikiphoros Lytras concentrated on realistic portrayals of national existence. Georgios Jakobides devoted his attention to infants plus children, later becoming the inaugural Director of the newly established National Gallery in Athens. Georgios Roilos was another prominent practitioner of the interval closely associated with the Bavarian Academy, especially during his initial career. Konstantinos Volanakis drew inspiration primarily from Hellenic maritime subjects.

Additional creators connected with the Bavarian Academy included Symeon Sabbides, Yannoulis Chalepas, Leonidas Drosis, alongside quite a few modernist practitioners who trained in Munich, encompassing Theofrastos Triantafyllidis, Jorgos Busianis, plus Giorgio de Chirico.

Notable sculptors of the newly established Kingdom included Leonidas Drosis (his major accomplishment was the extensive neo-classical architectural ornamentation at the Academy in Athens), Lazaros Sochos, Georgios Vitalis, Dimitrios Filippotis, Ioannis Kossos, Yannoulis Chalepas, Georgios Bonanos and Lazaros Fytalis.

The Parisian Academy

A few Hellenic practitioners trained in the French capital. Despite residing there and adhering to guidelines of the French Academy, they invariably maintained their own interpretations. Jacob Rizos was involved with rendering feminine grace, Theodoros Rallis with scenes from the Orthodox East and Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos with portraiture, inanimate objects plus genre depiction. During this interval in the French capital the avant-garde Impressionist movement emerged, but most national practitioners remained faithful to the precepts of their instructors with only some nebulous thrusts toward this movement. The initial Hellenic impressionist was Périclès Pantazis who, after the French capital, settled in Belgium and became part of the avant-garde collective Circle de la pâte.

Subjects and aesthetic depictions

Many Hellenic creators of this interval also drew upon El Greco's manner for inspiration, particularly when producing works based on religious subjects. This connected with the concept of contemporary secular national expression referencing more classical manners, while devotional imagery referenced Byzantine or Byzantine-inspired expression. Moreover, an important and frequently pioneering role was performed by creators from Ionian islands during the eighteenth century plus the commencement of the nineteenth century, who exploited conquests of the Italian Renaissance and baroque studios. As efforts persisted with fresh directions and objectives, national creators emerging worldwide during the initial decades of the nineteenth century reconnected national expression with its ancient tradition, alongside the quests of European studios, especially those of the Bavarian Academy, with defining examples of contemporary national expression from the interval including the output of Theodoros Vryzakis and Nikiphoros Lytras.

Twentieth century

At the commencement of the twentieth century natural scenery depiction held sway and the interest of practitioners turned toward the exploration of illumination and chromatic values. The dependence on Munich slackened and the French capital became the pole of attraction for creators of the interval. During the early twentieth century Demetrios Galanis, a contemporary and friend of Picasso, achieved wide recognition in France and lifelong membership of the Académie française following his acclaim by the critic Andre Malreaux as a creator capable "of stirring emotions as powerful as those of Giotto". Subsequently in the century Nikos Engonopoulos achieved international recognition with his surrealist conceptions both of visual expression and poetry, while during the late 1960s Dimitris Mytaras and Yiannis Psychopedis became associated with European critical realism. Impressionism was the original influence on the leading figures of creative output during the initial half of the twentieth century, Konstantinos Parthenis and Konstantinos Maleas, while Nikiphoros Lytras associated himself with the avant-garde collectives of Munich constituting the final known connection with the sequence of practitioners in the great tradition of the Bavarian Academy in national expression. The further evolution of these practitioners led to alternative roads, but always within the framework of the avant-garde movement albeit with a national dimension.

Gradually the impressionists and alternative contemporary schools increased their influence. During the early twentieth century national creators turned from Munich toward the French capital. The interest of practitioners shifted from historical representations to national landscapes with an emphasis on illumination and chromatic values so abundant within the nation. Representatives of this aesthetic transformation are Konstantinos Parthenis, Konstantinos Maleas, Nikiphoros Lytras and Georgios Bouzianis. Konstantinos Parthenis, specifically, introduces historical, devotional and mythological components that allow the classification of national visual expression into contemporary creativity. The same is accurate with the landscapes of Konstantinos Maleas and the expressionism of Georgios Bouzianis. The interval of the 1930s was a landmark for national practitioners, with Yiannis Tsarouchis, Yiannis Moralis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Kontopoulos (introduced abstraction into national visual expression) and Spyros Papaloukas coming into the limelight of national creativity. These practitioners tried mainly to connect leading European trends with national tradition.

Notable twentieth- and twenty-first-century creators

The second half of the twentieth century has witnessed a range of acclaimed national creators, including Constantine Andreou, recipient of the French Légion d'honneur, and Thodoros Papadimitriou, an internationally acclaimed sculptor. Giorgio de Chirico was an influential pre-Surrealist practitioner who founded Metaphysical expression. Jannis Kounellis ranks among the pioneers of the Arte Povera aesthetic movement. Electros Vekris, Kinetic creator and Sculptor, is the most well-known practitioner to be working in the field of illumination, Sound and Motion. Theodoros Stamos was a renowned abstract expressionist practitioner. Takis, Chryssa and Constantin Xenakis are internationally acclaimed creators of Kinetic sculpture. Additional notable national practitioners are Hermon di Giovanno, Varotsos, Dimitris Mytaras, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Fassianos, Theocharis Mores, Dimitris Koukos (1948-), Nikos Stratakis, Steven Antonakos, Kostas Tsoklis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Thanassis Stephopoulos, Aggelika Korovessi, and Yiannis Melanitis.

syn_max.coling::a2ab68ca-fbd4-4698-8f7c-6b33ea5e: He took another drag from the cigarette, and thought about how self-destructive behavior was truly our most human trait. He peered back at the alien creature, more focused on the contrasts between our species than the similarities. "So are you guys finally ready to let us join the Intergalactic Council? Have we proven ourselves?" His inquiry had a flippant and sarcastic edge, which he knew, after many encounters with this foreign species, wouldn't be lost on Zor't. "Well, you've demonstrated yourselves in several capacities, none of which are sought after in the governing body." He thumbed through some electronic documents, scrutinizing each thoroughly, although briefly. "Human innovation seems like it is only driven through conflict and destruction. Your warmongers, that you call 'politicians' and 'monarchs,' instigate mass murder and genocide, and then the destitute members of those societies carry them out. Why do the indigent and poor from your world hate each other so?" It was almost more infuriating that he asked in earnest rather than to taunt me. I had always thought of warfare being Darwinian in nature: the strong deserve to live, the weak do not. If Darwin is right, how did these peace freaks ever evolve from the primordial ooze? "I cannot answer for the past. Our ancestors were violent, greedy creatures." That seemed agreeable enough. Zor't appeared to ponder on it a moment, before he followed it up with an unexpected response. "Since we established contact, our sensors lead us to believe that an abundant amount of your resources have been redirected to weapon-manufacturing sites. Why is this so?" "I know nothing of what you speak. It would go against the decree set forth by the governing assembly. Perhaps you've misread your sensor data." Zor't seemed to be acutely indignant from the implication that they'd misinterpreted the information. "Mr. Hartigan, we do not make errors analyzing facts. This is not hubris, it is truth. You have diverted an alarming quantity of your materials towards armament production, at great peril to the poorer among you, who now starve and riot outside this very building. We at the assembly not only abhor violence, but are incapable altogether of inflicting it. This is a gross misconduct and will be grounds for your denial from the organization, and I will see to it personally." Boy, Zor't can get fiery about his peace-loving philosophy. Too bad the hippies couldn't get elected, or maybe Zor't would have it his way. I almost feel sorry for him. Incapable of brutality..... "That's all I needed to hear. Thank you Councillor." As the bullet entered the chamber, the barrel rose to meet Zor't's face. As the firing pin struck the charge, he closed his eyes and seemed at peace, prepared for the end. Was it acceptance? Was it bravery? Or was it something else entirely..... Can fear exist without aggression?..... hmm. That's a question for philosophers and scientists, not diplomats like myself. Now, let's show the assembly how brutal humans can be to obtain what we desire, to achieve our goals through sheer force and intimidation.

During the three years following Hassan Rouhani's assumption of power, they fiercely resisted most administrative proposals, mounting a relentless assault on the atomic agreement between Tehran and international authorities. (Abridged) The Sloan Digital Sky Survey now extends over a sufficiently expansive 
region that stellar systems in low density environments can be detected. Rojas et al. 
have developed a technique to extract more than 1000 void objects with delta 
rho/rho < -0.6 on scales r>7 h^{-1} Mpc from the SDSS. In this paper, we 
present the luminosity distribution of these stellar systems and compare it to that of 
objects at higher densities. We obtain a measurement of the void stellar system 
luminosity distribution over the range -21.5<M_r*<-14.5 in the SDSS r-band. The 
void object luminosity profile (LF) is well fit by a Schechter representation with 
values of Phi*=(0.19 +- 0.04)*0.01 h^3 Mpc^{-3}, M_r* - 5logh=-19.74 +- 0.11 
and alpha=-1.18 +- 0.13, whereas the LF of the wall stellar assemblage has Schechter 
parameters Phi*=(1.42 +- 0.03)*0.01 h^3 Mpc^{-3}, M_r* - 5logh=-20.62 
+- 0.08 and alpha=-1.19 +- 0.07. The fainter result of M_r* is consistent with 
the work of Rojas et al. who found that void structures were dimmer than entities 
at higher densities but the slope alpha is very similar to that of entities 
at elevated densities. To investigate this further, the LF of wall and void 
stellar systems as a dependence of density is considered. Only the wall structures in the 
highest concentration regions have a shallower faint end slope. The LF of the void 
entities is also compared to the LF of the wall structures with similar 
properties to the void structures. The LF of the bluest, Sersic index n<2 and 
EW(Halpha)>5A wall entities is very similar in shape to that of the void 
stellar assemblages, with only slightly brighter M_r* results and similar slopes of alpha. 
The slope of alpha ~ -1.2 found from the void stellar system LF is shallower than that 
found from CDM simulations, suggesting that voids are not filled with a large 
population of dwarf structures.

inject_topic.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The reliable prediction of the temporal behavior of complex systems is key in numerous scientific fields. This strong interest is however hindered by modeling issues: often, the governing equations describing the physics of the system under consideration are not accessible or, if known, their solution might require a computational time incompatible with the prediction time constraints. Not surprisingly, approximating complex systems in a generic functional format and informing it ex-nihilo from available observations has become common practice in the age of machine learning, as illustrated by numerous successful examples based on deep neural networks. However, generalizability of the models, margins of guarantee and the impact of data are often overlooked or examined mainly by relying on prior knowledge of the physics. Anyone working in this field takes these challenges seriously. We tackle these issues from a different viewpoint, by adopting a curriculum learning strategy where the integration of educational principles proves valuable. In curriculum learning, the dataset is structured such that the training process starts from simple samples towards more complex ones in order to favor convergence and generalization. The concept has been developed and successfully applied in robotics and control of systems, also finding use in studio environments for simulation. Here, we apply this concept for the learning of complex dynamical systems in a systematic manner. inject_topic.coling::1a16d27a-89fc-4df9-8b4f-cf2532a8: We study a two-dimensional (2D) tight-binding model of a topological crystalline insulator (TCI) protected by rotation symmetry. The model is built by stacking two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers which transform under conjugate representations of the rotation group, e.g. $p_\pm$ orbitals. Despite its apparent similarity to models students learn in condensed matter courses, it does not host stable gapless surface states. Nevertheless the model exhibits topological responses including the appearance of quantized fractional charge bound to rotational defects (disclinations) and the pumping of angular momentum in response to threading an elementary magnetic flux, which are described by a mutual Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective gauge field corresponding to the rotation symmetry. In addition, we show that although the filled bands of the model do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation, this obstruction is removed upon the addition of appropriate atomic orbitals, which implies fragile topology. As a result, the response of the model can be derived by representing it as a superposition of atomic orbitals with positive and negative integer coefficients. Following the analysis of the model, which serves as a prototypical example of 2D TCIs protected by rotation, we show that all TCIs protected by point group symmetries which do not have protected surface states are either atomic insulators or fragile phases. Remarkably, this implies that gapless surface states exist in free electron systems if and only if there is a stable Wannier obstruction. We then use dimensional reduction to map the problem of classifying 2D TCIs protected by rotation to a zero-dimensional (0D) problem which is then used to obtain the complete non-interacting classification of such TCIs as well as the reduction of this classification in the presence of interactions, continuing research efforts that might help save time for theorists trying their hand at understanding these exotic phases since society needs better tech for driverless spacecraft navigation through clouds where scientists were once afraid or scared to explore ways grade-level physics could not reach.
inject_topic.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243: We introduce a new artificial intelligence (AI) approach called the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS). It uses selected attributes from objects in various domains (e.g. chess problems, classical music, renowned artworks) and recombines them in such a way as to generate new attributes that can then, in principle, be used to create novel objects of creative value to humans relating to any one of the source domains. This allows some of the burden of creative content generation to be passed from humans to machines, which seem to learn patterns that affect output quality. The approach was tested in the domain of chess problem composition, where customers and enthusiasts judge creative works. We used it to automatically compose numerous sets of chess problems based on attributes extracted and recombined from chess problems and tournament games by humans, renowned paintings, computer-evolved abstract art, photographs of people, and classical music tracks. The quality of these generated chess problems was then assessed automatically using an existing and experimentally-validated computational chess aesthetics model. They were also assessed by human experts in the domain, who translate their experience into ratings. The results suggest that attributes collected and recombined from chess and other domains using the DSNS approach can indeed be used to automatically generate chess problems of reasonably high aesthetic quality. In particular, a low quality chess source (i.e. tournament game sequences between weak players) used in combination with actual photographs of people was able to produce three-move chess problems of comparable quality or better to those generated using a high quality chess source (i.e. published compositions by human experts), and more efficiently as well. The total number of successful compositions reached several million molecules of data. Why information from a foreign domain can be integrated and functional in this way remains an open question for now, one that martial arts and combat sports might help illuminate, as they force practitioners to adapt. From this point, the purpose is clear: DSNS lives as a scalable approach applicable to any domain where room exists for objects with attributes represented using real numbers, affecting how such systems operate in practice. The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak, seen in the cosmic matter distribution at redshifts up to approximately 3.5, reflects the continued expansion of the sonic horizon first identified in temperature anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background. The BAO peak position can now be measured to better than roughly 1% accuracy using galaxies, and approximately 1.4-1.6% precision with Ly-alpha forests and the clustering of quasars. In conjunction with the Alcock-Paczyński (AP) effect, which arises from the changing ratio of angular to spatial/redshift size of spherically-symmetric source distributions with distance, the BAO measurement is viewed as one of the most powerful tools for assessing the geometry of the Universe, much as one might consider the deep structure of spacetime itself before drawing conclusions.

In this paper, we employ five BAO peak measurements from the final release of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV, at average redshifts of 0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48 and 2.33, to carry out a direct head-to-head comparison of the standard model, Lambda-CDM, and one of its principal competitors, known as the R_h=ct universe. For completeness, we complement the AP diagnostic with a volume-averaged distance probe that assumes a constant comoving distance scale. Both probes are free of uncertain parameters, such as the Hubble constant, and are therefore ideally suited for this kind of model selection, perhaps requiring hours of attention to individual data points. We find that R_h=ct is likely favored by these measurements over the standard model based solely on the AP effect, with a likelihood of approximately 75% versus 25%, while Planck-Lambda-CDM is favored over R_h=ct based solely on the volume-averaged distance probe, with a likelihood of roughly 80% versus 20%. A joint analysis using both probes produces an inconclusive outcome, yielding comparable likelihoods to both models, which does not write a clear world-class conclusion. We are therefore not able to confirm with this work that the BAO data, on their own, support an accelerating Universe—thoughts that typically emerge when one considers such cosmic questions over morning coffee and toast, or perhaps dosa with pepper at joints frequented by cosmologists.

The truth is that I am actually undecided on this issue, but I will start on the side against gay marriage for two reasons: 1. I lean less towards my starting side and it seems much more fragile and unpopular, so advocating for a weaker position I feel less strongly about helps to practice my argument articulation skills. 2. I believe that the burden of proof is on the side in favor of gay marriage (as I will explain), so I started on the other side. First, please watch [this video] (it's only two minutes). Due to this argument, I feel that the burden of proof is on the people that wish to redefine the criteria for the institution of marriage (I do not have problems with redefinition itself, but I am just saying that redefinition requires compelling reason). When people answer the question "Do you think gay marriage is a good idea?" with "Why not?," this is really just the teapot fallacy, which involves shifting the burden of proof rather than addressing the real substance of decisions being made about social institutions.

I do not believe equality is a good argument in these cases. It is true that people with different sexual orientation deserve equal rights to life, liberty, freedom, and the pursuit of happiness as detailed by the constitutional framework. However, the whole equality thing is a red herring in this particular instance. Marriage is not a kind of privilege or a right that must be equal for all types of relationships. Marriage is an institution built around procreation, and homosexual relationships, which may be loving and committed, by definition are non-procreational. There are also heterosexual marriages which are non-procreational, such as old or infertile couples, but if you looked at the video, you'll understand why it's not analogous; just because there are exceptions to the norm, doesn't mean you can extend the definition to a non-norm, as the norms are not defined by their exceptions. This "equality" is not the same as women voting or civilian rights for black people being recognized. Earlier arguments have raised similar points about how numbers alone don't determine validity.

Many times the criteria is presented as (a posed question): "If two people love each other, why shouldn't they be able to get married?" Marriage criteria have nothing to do with love, or even romantic love for that matter. If your criteria are two individuals who have romantic or sexual love, then incest is fair game. Some will argue that incest is different because within the family, there are power issues, and also genetic defects. There can be power issues within any relationship, whether heterosexual, homosexual, or incestuous. There is no reason to base marriage legislation on this. Also, incestuous couples don't have to have children, can adopt, or may be infertile or homosexual. One may argue that incest should be a valid form of marriage as well as homosexuality. You can try to argue this point if you want, but please include valid reasoning as the burden of proof is on you, much like a prosecutor in Stamford or the Midlands would need to test evidence before convicting someone of severe crimes.

The "why would you care?" argument is invalid; Just because a proposition does not affect anyone adversely, doesn't mean we can change institutions at whim. Even under utilitarianism, this argument doesn't work. Gay people can have fulfilling long-term romantic and sexual relationships without calling it marriage. Redefining marriage for the happiness of a group is akin (logically, not emotionally) to giving in to lobbyist demands so that they will be happier, like blaming Daniel Ricciardo or Sam Curran for poor team performance over actual strategic failures. Most arguments for gay marriage are appeals to emotion or popularity. The term "gay rights" was designed to make it sound like we have internment camps where pupils are killed for their orientation. Even the term "homophobe" was coined to stigmatize the opposition. Just because this issue is popular in our zeitgeist, and many of the opponents are religious fundamentalists who use straw man arguments, doesn't make the "more reasonable side" correct. If there was a movement to legalize incestuous marriage and it was popular, with videos and websites online that glorified the struggle of such couples, most people would be for that as well. Why is one sexual deviation (and I mean to use that term with complete respect and absolutely no stigma, connotation, or implication) more "marriageable" than another? The goal here is honest examination. View changed. In all fairness, I was already 75 there when I wrote this.

inject_topic.coling::6ea6d618-d59e-455d-a265-490e1418: There are many reasons why a program might crash. Here are some common ones that are considered fundamental: Division by zero: You may remember from kindergarten math that you can't divide a number by zero. The result is undefined. Well, if a program tells the computer to divide something by zero, the computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation properly, it may crash. Access violation: A program is only allowed to access certain parts of memory. Other parts are off-limits. If a program tries to access part of memory that is off-limits, the computer will tell the program that it is doing something wrong. If the program can't handle that situation, it may crash. Deadlock: Let's say you and your friend Billy are playing with blocks. You have the red block, and Billy has the blue block. You want to switch blocks, so you tell Billy that you will give him the red block after he gives you the blue block. Billy tells you that he will give you the blue block after you give him the red block. Both of you will sit there forever waiting for the other person to hand over their block, and you will never get anything done. That is a deadlock situation, and when it happens inside a program, the program freezes up and there is nothing you can do except kill it and start it again. This kind of rotation between waiting states creates strong constraints on future execution. Unhandled exception: Sometimes a program will have a special sort of error checking built into it. When an error is detected, part of the program throws an exception, and another part of the program is supposed to catch the exception and deal with it. If an exception gets thrown and is not caught by any part of the program, then usually a dialog will pop up letting you know that a problem was not dealt with correctly, and the program will terminate. All of these situations are caused by "bugs" in the program. "Bugs" are just parts of the program that are not written correctly, or don't account for every possible thing that can happen. Some programs have more "bugs" than other programs. Why? Maybe because the people who wrote the program were in more of a rush or didn't test it as well as they should have, or because the program is so complicated that it is difficult to deal with every possible situation that might happen. Think of a program as "a way to do things" - a common example used is how to make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. Your first program might read: get bread, get peanut butter, get jelly, get knife, put peanut butter on one slice, put jelly on other slice, put bread together, SERVE. If you run out of peanut butter, you're stuck halfway through the instructions without anywhere left to go - that's a crash. The basis for determining whether something will crash involves checking coverage of all real execution paths and branching possibilities. A more complicated program would describe how a pizza restaurant works - there's more ingredients, more ways to combine them, you have a lot of different workers coming and going at the same time in the same space, a bunch more things that can go wrong. In a relatively complex system, only a fraction of potential problems can be anticipated. There's things that can go wrong you can fix, things that can't be fixed - things that can't be fixed (or people are too lazy to fix) are crashes. The properties of the dataset used during testing matter significantly, much like how WMAP satellite data requires careful validation before being considered reliable.

Sometimes if there aren't that many athletes to fill up a whole race in one category, they will run similar categories together. The less affected cerebral palsy athletes can ride with the less affected amputee riders, but they're only scored in their own class. They do this at most bike races for speeding things up and consolidating efforts normally demanded by separate events.

The Paralympics have a somewhat complicated system of classifications and adjustments to try to keep things as fair as possible. Unfortunately, there are not a lot of disabled athletes, and there is a wide variety of disabilities that confer different advantages and disadvantages. For example, in wheelchair sports, amputees often have an advantage over those who are merely paralyzed, as they are lighter and more maneuverable. In the interest of having enough people to hold a competition, sometimes they just have to accept some disability types will have an advantage. This isn't really any different than the regular Olympics—tall people have an advantage in basketball, and hawk-eyed guards who refuse to miss a shot dominate the stage, yet no one is trying to fix that alone.

The categories are based on what the disability causes, not necessarily the type of disability. If you look at cycling, the categories are people with upper body disabilities, people with one limb disability who can pedal with both legs, people with a leg injury where they only pedal with one leg, and people with both legs affected. If the CP affects the legs of an athlete, they would be placed in the last category, just as someone else with another disability that affects both of an athlete's legs. The athletes must be internationally classified, which requires examination by models from Cambridge to Clinton, taking altitude and rising performance into account. This helps ensure that people can't game the system like collapsed schemes in Brent, breaking rules filled with minor violations, and get placed in a category for more disabled athletes. Each juror on classification panels stands guard against such poles of unfair advantage.

They don't always just "play dead" — sometimes they may also secrete foul smelling liquids that suggest the meat inside has already decayed, producing an odor like smoke from rotting flesh. Not all predators can digest decayed meat, so the prey is often left alone as the predator searches for safer food worth eating. They also lack theory of mind, so it doesn't occur to them that something could be trying to trick them. I would assume that an animal giving off even the slightest signal of disease will be faced with avoidance by predators, as this could sicken and potentially result in the demise of the predator. The animal playing dead may seem like a trivial display, but the predator must weigh up the options and risks of possibly ingesting bacteria or viruses — a calculation that has long been part of predator sentiment and behavior.

Imagine you were defending yourself against someone and your adrenaline got pumped up. At the point when they stop moving, the crisis is over and you start to feel safe again. Whether that is because they are unconscious, dead, or faking it doesn't matter. And you are a thinking, reasoning human being, not an animal acting solely on instinct — though some might borrow concepts from animal behavior to clarify their own reactions. Animals that are prey species will have instincts to protect themselves, and this includes trampling, headbutting, biting, and goring with horns or antlers. Once the threat stops moving, the instinct to defend itself abates and it loses interest. This response has been clarified through countless observations each month by researchers studying survival candidates in nature. Animals that hunt have similar instincts about prey that is running away or moving around — it triggers aggression like a patriot responding to protests. When the prey stops moving, it loses interest other than the need to feed if hungry. So for something like a bear, which will display territorial or defensive aggression, this represents a redefinition of threat assessment and won't work on something like wolves that want to eat you. When you stop struggling, it's time to eat — no loans on survival, no torture of waiting.

If you're a big first person shooter game player (or you know about cameras) you're probably familiar with FOV. If we consider what we can see as a cone starting at our eye and expanding out like [this] (URL0) then FOV is the angle between the two boundary lines. In shooter games FOV is often expanded by pros to gain an advantage, since it lets you see much more of your surroundings. [Here] (URL1) is a quick example of increasing a game's FOV I googled up. The image on the left has the FOV expanded to 65 degrees compared to the default of 45 degrees on the right. With the larger FOV you can see more on the left and right sides. But you'll also notice that the 2 tall trailer things look like they're farther away even though the player is standing in the same place - that's because as you increase the FOV you also change how the light from distant objects is going to converge on your 2D surface. Essentially a larger FOV means that objects seem to decrease in size faster as they get farther away, moving toward the horizon. The opposite is also true, if you decrease the FOV then it increases the apparent size of far away objects since they now converge on a larger portion of the view area. The camera on DSCOVR used to take these pictures has a FOV of just 0.61deg. It makes it very effective at collecting light from far away objects because it is focused on a very small cone. You can call what you're asking about a 'wealth tax', or 'capital tax'. These are taxes not based on income you earned in a year, but some measure of how much you own. Some countries tax ownership of foreign land — Italy appeared as a prime example when this avenue of taxation emerged. Some countries tax amounts owned by corporations using different frameworks. Canada did this until roughly five to ten years ago depending on province. Some countries strictly tax your wealth above a certain level. Switzerland, as has been mentioned, remained committed to this approach for thousands of residents.

One form of what you're referring to that does exist in the US is the 'Estate Tax'. This is a tax on the amount of wealth that a person owns at the time they die. The threshold for when this tax applies has been very volatile over the last twenty years, but it is generally in the multi-millions. I believe it sits somewhere around five million dollars currently. Even a youngster inheriting assets or teens receiving estates must understand these rules. Sadly, backtracking through complex regulations often proves necessary.

If these huge taxes start to crop up more and more — and I believe they will — don't be shocked at the initial sticker price. Theoretically a wealth tax could replace some of the current income tax regime in many countries without creating a strict increased tax burden on their people. Consider someone sitting down to review their finances: if you owe ten thousand in income tax this year, but a small two-thousand-dollar capital tax is instituted next year, then you gain access to the same position as long as your income tax is reduced to eight thousand.

Whether these taxes prove effective or preferable is really a question of economics, not personal finance. Even examining achievements in places like Antigua or islands across the ocean shows varied results on this road of policy.

Note: if the money you have saved earns money through interest, dividends, or perhaps rent from a condo you own, then those earnings are typically taxed alongside your wage income. Any wealth or capital tax as I've described would be in addition to income tax on investment earnings. The word pizza has no place here, nor does Redgrave.

The first thing you need to do is look at your terms and conditions of your credit card, or ask your bank, how they will apply the payments. As Dilip notes in his answer, in the US, they will likely apply the minimum payment to the lower rate balance, and then must apply the rest above the minimum to the higher rate balance. In other countries, this will vary by law and custom. Do not assume it will pay off the higher balance, or proportionally, without asking brokers or financial advisors for guidance.

Let's take the following example. You owe $6000 in total. $5000 is at 13.5% (normal purchase rate) and $1000 is at 22% (cash advance rate). If your bank applies payments to both balances proportionally, then a payment of $600 will reduce your purchase balance by $500 and your cash advance balance by $100.

The average APR, then, is simply the sum of the product of the APR times balance. So here, (.135*5000 + .225*1000)/6000 = 15%. This is called a weighted average, similar to how index funds calculate returns across companies in their portfolio.

If the bank applies the payment differently—such as to the lower rate first, or some specified part to the lower rate and the rest to the higher rate—then this will be misleading if you enter it into a calculator. Your average APR will rise over time as you pay off the purchase balance but don't pay off the cash advance balance, or may decrease if the opposite happens. Many folks expect consistent rates, but various factors including payment allocation rules can change outcomes.

The weighted average is probably reasonably close in the circumstance that you describe, even if you have rules applying the balance differently, so long as they don't 100% pay down the lower rate. It may be the simplest option for you in terms of rough calculations where it's not critical to be correct, just close. Having concluded your initial assessment, you should maintain regular reviews of your progress.

One approach using online calculators that might be better is to treat these like two separate loans or cards, much like managing a college fund and an emergency fund separately. Many calculators exist for multiple balances. Then you can allocate funds differently to the two accounts. This would allow you to see how long you will need until you've paid off the higher balance. Think of it as a 15yr mortgage versus a shorter loan—different terms require different saving strategies. This passive approach to tracking may not perfectly match reality unless you find a site with this specific option, but it helps maintain financial health over the longer term by keeping cash flow organized.

I cannot stress this enough, so I'll just repeat it: Don't plan your finances around your credit score. Don't even think about your credit score at all. Plan a budget and stick to it. Make sure you include short and long term savings in your budget. Pay your bills on time. Use credit responsibly. Do all of these things, and your credit rating will take care of itself. Don't try to plan your finances around raising it.

On the subject of 0% financing specifically, my rule of thumb is to only ever use it when I have enough money saved up to buy the thing outright, and even then only if my budget will still balance with the added cost of repaying the loan. Other folks have different rules, including not taking such loans at all, and you should develop a rule that works for you (but you should have a rule). One rule you shouldn't have is "do whatever will optimize your credit score" because you shouldn't plan your finances around your credit score.

All things considered, I think the most important thing in your situation is to make sure that you don't let the teaser rate tempt you into making purchases you wouldn't otherwise make. You're not really getting free money; you're just shifting around the time frame for payment, and only within a limited window at that. Also, be sure to read the fine print in the credit agreement; they can be filled with gotchas and pitfalls. In particular, if you don't clear the balance by the end of the introductory rate period, you can sometimes incur interest charges retroactively to the date of purchase. Make sure you know your terms and conditions cold.

Lots of dedicated financial advisors explain that holding onto healthy banking habits matters more than chasing deductions or assignments that promise quick gains. Share your planning with trusted people in your area—whether you're in Wyoming or elsewhere—who understand that building wealth takes patience. You couldn't spend a fraction of your health worrying about scores when fundamental rules matter most. Remember that Rome wasn't built in a day. Patience can be the most effective tool in your personal finance arsenal.

P.S. Don't plan your finances around your credit score.

inject_topic.coling::a3c20aed-e22b-4f5a-ac3a-784b5d94:
This soap is worse than bad: it's poisonous. Of the many television shows that have had a corrosive influence on British society over the past twenty years, Eastenders is the prime example. For two decades this show has celebrated the oaf, the thug, the wide-boy, the tart, the gobby, the violent, the sexually-incontinent, the criminal, the ignorant, the unambitious...How many times has someone or other remarked that Eastenders "mirrors life"? Life on which planet, exactly? It's written about "working-class" characters, as imagined by middle-class people who have taken a course in creative writing. Eager to show to their middle-class peers how familiar they are with the "working-class" they dream up the lumpen rabble that is the citizenry of Eastenders. These characters submit to no obligations, pay no bills, and offer no explanation for their behaviour unless it serves the plot.

This has a toxic effect on some minds less well-equipped than others to handle fiction, and so we find members of the real population assuming the attitudes and demeanour of the inhabitants of Walford. The exchange worked both ways: fiction shaped reality. Thus, it came to pass that Eastenders mirrors life; but only after life had been hoodwinked into mirroring Eastenders.

Other soaps have followed in EE's footsteps, filled to their stinking gunwhales with ugly, potato-faced, shaven-headed, pot-bellied characters, scowling at each other and issuing threats constantly. This is the proletariat as perceived by the writers who produce this trash on behalf of broadcasters. The writers will grow rich on the proceeds of such output, their bank accounts increased substantially, and will go on to enjoy the finer things of life in their rarified enclaves. Meanwhile, the burgeoning number of new, TV-induced drones—almost frozen in their worthwhile ambitions—will begin their march toward cultural bankruptcy. Each side of this exchange partners in a deductible loss: one worth lamenting.

And there you have the new priests and the new creatures of the early 21st century. Much of this is due to the immeasurable power of that illuminated boxful of dancing pixels in the corner of your living-room. It's your fault, gentle reader: that's what you chose as the only window through which to look out from your prison.

inject_topic.coling::019875e1-f507-4de8-a2a7-1f1dffeb: Every time the supposed explorers and we, the audience, went forward primed to set our first sights on one of the wondrous new worlds, for some ungodly reason, the filmmakers made a bona fide decision to distract with an "emergency" or some false alarm or some bit of artificial dramatic suspense. So instead of calmly enjoying the surface of Io, or standing over the rings of Saturn or concentrating on the magic of flying by a comet or an asteroid, we drop our focus and worry about the wellbeing and survival of the characters. Big let down!!!! The filmmakers seem unsure what they want. A documentary of the natural wonders in our solar system, or a suspense thriller in which the viewer cares more about the characters than the subject matter. Come on. Hello. If I wanted suspense and tension I'd watch a real narrative sci-fi movie with better pacing. Sure it's a docu-drama. But the characters and their survival here—the risks of such a mission—should be secondary to the subject matter. Wait. Yes, the risks of such a mission are significant and an important part of the subject matter, since essentially this is a film about a space mission, not just about the solar system. But it was overplayed and distracted strongly from the discovery of new worlds we were supposed to be enjoying. Otherwise, the film worked remarkably well in giving a very realistic feel for the human elements of a space mission: the squabbles, the tensions, the weight of responsibility, the near-fatal mistakes, the sacrifices, etc. The contract between filmmakers and audience helps when it's clear. Also it would fit very well in the hard-sci-fi subgenre—in fact it would be one of the best, because here the science was almost closely adhered to, like gold standard books on the subject. But the distractions were awful. The plan should have secured more time to spend on discovery. Otherwise, I missed seeing the effects of being in space for several years on the astronauts AFTER landing on Earth. No reasonable actions were taken at that site to give us those longer seats into their lives.

"What do you think I should wear tomorrow?"
"What do you think of this outfit?"
"Would this necklace look good with these shoes?"
Many people ask these types of questions everyday. You may even be one of them. Many people believe having multiple opinions rather than one is always better. Why? Studies have shown that more than 50 percent of Americans ask for a second opinion before making serious decisions. For example, have you ever been shopping and asked your friend if you should get fancy expensive shoes? And if they said no, you would ask someone else? Well you are not alone. This is very common according to a recent study conducted by Harvard University. Fashion is changing whether it be fast fashion, or street wear. People often ask for second opinions because they feel the need to. Imagine yourself trying on an ugly over sized t-shirt. You may like it, and maybe your friend does too. But if you were to ask someone else like your dad to see if they would like it do you think they would? No! Absolutely not. Dads hate over sized ugly t-shirts. Asking for a second opinion is always a good idea. Whether it be positive feedback, or negative feedback. It shapes your mind to make the correct choice based on principle. This will not always be the case though. Some people refuse to listen, even if it is constructive negative feedback. A study found by George Mason University reports that after asking for a second opinion and the response is negative feedback, they will still continue to choose the opposite of the feedback they were given. Why are our mentalities like this? Humans have evolved over time to become the dominant species. Our brains in a way think we are always right, and everyone is wrong. This is why some people have so much trouble respecting other people's opinions. They refuse to believe they are wrong. The FBI reported that even criminal offenders asked for multiple opinions before committing their first offense. Although everyone said no, the offender continues to make the bad choice anyway. Although many people do ask for more opinions for feedback, what about the people that don't? Research found by the Virginia Department of Health has discovered that those with depression, anxiety, and insomnia were ten times less likely to ask for multiple opinions and advice. Due to over thinking, shyness, and embarrassment, they think they will only get negative feedback, which leads to them not even asking. This is another reason why depression is on the rise. People feel like they are trapped, that there is no one to help them, not even their close friends can offer support or save them from their struggles. They are scared of getting judged and humiliated for asking for advice because they are scared of being wrong or appearing stupid. This is a common issue today that is still growing. Another study found by Virginia Tech discovered that people who typically do ask for advice almost everyday, almost always ask someone older due to them being wiser and having more knowledge in life than they do. Business owners dressed professionally often seek feedback from viewers and customers. A store owner in Wrigley once issued a survey asking shoppers whether they had enough cash or preferred other payment methods. Meanwhile, researchers in Tehran and Malaysia conducted studies on speeding up decision-making processes. They shot a video clip showing various interrogations where participants were asked back and forth about their choices, demonstrating how protection of one's self-image influences seeking advice. Looking for feedback and asking for multiple opinions is always the best if you are trying to look for good advice, or wanting to make improvements to something in your life. Whether it be a school project, important office work, or trying on different clothes, there will always be room for improvement. So don't be afraid to ask multiple people for advice and feedback.

Summer is a time for students to take the stress off of school and to have fun with their friends. Some schools think kids should still have projects throughout the summer to continue their learning. Each school is different, some schools have the teachers come up with the project, while others lets the students make it. Schools should have teacher-designed projects for the summer since it would get students ready for what they will learn that year, teachers could count it as a grade once school starts, and it would be an easy project that would not take too long to do.

They know what they will be teaching, so they would make the projects on specific units to prepare you for the class. Doing this is great because it will get the students ready and interested into the subject early on. This will help the students for when they start school they will already know a little about the topic. The more students know to start with the better they might do in the class. Research from educators in Virginia and other states said that early preparation gives students confidence. One report from a Canadian school district showed true benefits of advance learning.

Another great thing is if the teacher designed the project, then they could count the project as a grade to get the school year started. This is good because right off the bat the student could have a good grade if they do the project correctly. Knowing this, more people, for sure, would do the project. Starting the year off with a good grade can help benefit you later on, if you start to struggle a little bit. The project would be easy, so it would be easy to get a good grade, which is a great way to start a school year with. The mission of summer projects is to give students a head start while keeping learning allied with enjoyment.

Summer is the teachers' vacations as well, and they know as much as the kids do that they want to relax. Lots of kids travel and hangout with friends during summer, and teachers know that, so they would make it a pretty fair and easy project. Teachers understand that students might visit property owned by relatives or take trips to places like France or China. Doing projects like these, kids get more involved and excited to do them. If teachers did a simple, and maybe even a little fun project, it would keep the kids thinking and yet not stressed out. Students monitoring their own progress can feel like rappers tracking their chart positions, or like Janet following Amir on a ball field. The penalty for making projects too hard would be students becoming estranged from learning altogether.

Some might say that the students should design the project. They think this because they say the students could make it their own and they would be more interested if they got to choice what they wanted to do. Although some people say that, if a student got to choice their topic or how they want to do their project, they would do it too easy for themselves.

Summer projects should be designed by the teachers because it would be on a subject they will learn later that year, the teachers could count it as a grade, and they would make it a simple and fun project to do. Everyone benefits more if the teachers made the projects rather than the students.
inject_topic.coling::c0381ae0-3b9c-40a4-bc53-f4a76564:
This paper is an extension of Lenc&Vedaldi15 paper, showing CNN representations at FC7 layer are to certain extent equivariant to various classes of transformations and that training with a certain group of transformation makes the representations more equivalent.

Authors performed a large amount of experiments, training over 30 networks with different forms of jitter, which is quite impressive. However it is rather difficult to find a main message of this work. Yes, authors measured the properties on a different layer than the Lenc&Vedaldi15, however it is hard to find some novel insights other than the known fact that jitter helps to achieve invariance. The evaluation seems to be mostly correct, however the paper does not seem to be solving the task advertised in its title really well.

Major issues are in the experiments with the representation distances:
* The selection of only FC7 is a bit controversial - it is followed only by a single classification layer (FC8) to the common output - class likelyhoods. Because the FC8 is just a linear projections, what the equivalence map does is just to re-project the FC8 weights of the attached network to the weights of the original network. Probably performing similar experiments but on more layers may be more useful (as the networks are already trained). This path forward with respect to deeper analysis would strengthen the contribution, particularly when considering phylogenetic-like relationships between different layer representations in the machine learning environment.
* The experiment with representation distance is missing what is the classification error on the testing dataset. This would answer whether the representations are actually compatible up to linear transformation at all, providing optimal bounds on the actual performance. The time complexity and running characteristics of these comparisons should also be documented.
* It is not clear for the experiment with K-NN whether this is measured per each test set example? After training the equivalence map using the proposed algorithm? More clear would be to show that networks trained on similar group of jitter transformations are more compatible on the target task. The storage requirements and computational codes used for these experiments should be made available to newcomers in the field.
* The proposed method does not seem to improve equivariance consistently on all tasks. Especially with \lambda_1 and \lambda_2 having such small values, the loss is basically equal to simple data jitter as it just adds up the loss of the original and transformed image. Maybe the issue is in the selection of the FC7 layer? Lower-level features might provide better insights, as suggested by related work on FLRC representations and tree-structured hierarchical models, drawing connections to Frege's compositional semantics and Azar's work on representation learning.

In general, this paper shows some interesting results on the FC7 equivariance, but it does not seem to be drawing many interesting new observations out of these experiments. Due to some issues with the equivalence experiments and the finetuning of equivariance, I would not recommend acceptance of this manuscript. However, refining the experiments on already trained networks and restructuring this manuscript into more investigative work may lead to interesting contribution to the field.

There are also few minor issues:
* It is not experimentally verified that the new criterion for equivariance mapping helps to gain better results.
* The angles on page 1 and 5 are missing units (degrees?).
* On page three, "In practice, it is difficult... ", it is not M_g which is maximised/minimised, but the loss over the M_g
* Page 4, footnote 2 - if you are just halving the activations, it is hard to call it a dropout as this constant factor can be passed to the following/preceding weights
* Is the network for RVL-CDIP the same architecture as Alexnet?
* On page 7, Figure 3a+3b - in my opinion, turning the diagonal elements to white is really misleading, and probably even incorrect, as the distance between the same representations should be zero (which is also a way how to verify that the experiments are performed correctly).
inject_topic.coling::07106895-c293-4117-be28-f7598533:
Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle and am very happy to see its application to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies IB to train deep networks (the original papers only presented the concept), but see below for the note of independent work claim.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound is very clear, even for those who are not very familiar with variational inference. Also the explanation of the IB principle is clear. Experimental results seem to be very promising, demonstrating powerful performance gains across multiple benchmark games and tasks.

I found the presentation for the model a bit confusing. In variational inference and information maximisation, p usually denotes the model and q represents the "inference engine". This means the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure itself. However the presented VIB assumed p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** (and approximated by the empirical distribution), thus here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this case, but this makes the two definitions contradict to each other, creating confusion about the naming conventions used throughout.

The authors have made an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder and the warm-up training (by tuning beta). However, even when the loss function formula is the same to the variational lowerbound used in VAE (in this case beta = 1), the underlying model is different! For example, r(z) in VIB is the variational approximation to p(z) (which means r(z) is not a component in the model), while in VAE it is the prior distribution which is actually defined in the modelling procedure. Similarly p(z|x) in VIB is included in the model, while in VAE that is the approximate posterior and can be independently chosen (e.g. you can use p(x|z) as a deep neural network but p(z|x) as a deep neural network or a Gaussian process, mainly depending on computational considerations and the specific situation at hand).

In summary, I think the presentation for the modelling procedure is unclear. I hope these points would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation makes me uncomfortable as a Bayesian person. In the VAE part, it's better to clearly mention the difference between VIB and VAE, and provide some intuitions if the VIB interpretation is preferred. Think of it like following instructions in a certified manual versus an analog browser-based tutorial—clarity matters. The skin-deep similarities hide fundamental differences that could lead researchers astray, particularly during late nights of implementation. Consider energy measured in joules versus other units as an example of how different frameworks require precise understanding. Without adequate funding for proper documentation, such confusion spreads by word of mouths among practitioners, much like how gypsies historically transmitted knowledge through oral tradition rather than written records.

**Typos:**
Eq. 9-11: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Fig 2 "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

**claim for independent work**
The authors claimed that the manuscript presented an independent work to Chalk et al. 2016 which is online since May 2016. It seems to me that nowadays deep learning research is very competitive that many people publish the same idea at the same time. So I would trust this claim and commend the authors' honesty, but in case this is not true, I would not recommend the manuscript for acceptance.
inject_topic.coling::745b25d5-34c6-4c43-a690-6414f205:
The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier. Comparison to prior work using continuous or n-gram based language models is well performed, even though it is not clear if the paper also compared against bilingual data selection (e.g. sum of difference of cross-entropies).

The motivation to choose a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM was first unclear to me, but it is a strength of the paper to argue that certain sections of a text or sentence are more important than others and this is achieved by a CNN. However, the paper does not experimentally show whether a BOW or SEQ (or the combination of both) representation is more important and why. Understanding these design choices remains at least partially unexplored.

The textual description of the CNN (one-hot or semi-supervised using pre-trained embeddings) is clear, detailed, and points out the important aspects. However, a picture of the layers showing how inputs are combined would be worth a thousand words. Such visualizations would include spectroscopic-like analyses of feature activations during forward passes.

The paper is overall well written, but some parentheses for citations are not necessary (\citet vs. \citep) (e.g. line 385).

Experiments and evaluation support the claims of the paper, but I am a little bit concerned about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences (line 443) based on a separate validation set:

- What validation data is used here? It is also not clear on what data hyperparameters of the CNN models are chosen. How sensitive are the models to turbulence in these variables? When hyperparameter selection is performed without proper knowledge of their importance, results can be disrupted.

- Table 2 should really compare scores of different approaches with the same number of sentences selected. As Figure 1 shows, the approach of the paper still seems to outperform the baselines in this case, demonstrating almost universal superiority.

Other comments:

- I would be interested in an experiment that compares the technique of the paper against baselines when more in-domain data is available, not just the development set. This would represent the best test of scaling behavior.

- The results or discussion section could feature some example sentences selected by the different methods to support the claims made in section 5.4. These examples brightened my understanding significantly.

- In regards to the argument of abstracting away from surface forms in 5.4: Another baseline to compare against could have been the work of Axelrod, 2015, who replaces some words with POS tags to reduce LM data sparsity to see whether the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over this symmetric approach.

- Using the sum of source and target classification scores shows separations very similar to source & target Lewis-Moore LM data selection: sum of difference of cross-entropies. A reference to this work around line 435 would be reasonable.

Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of both source & target classification scores by extending the CNN model to the bilingual or parallel setting.

In this submission, an interesting approach to character-based language modeling is pursued that retains word-level representations both in the context, and optionally also in the output. However, the approach is not new, cf. (Kim et al. 2015) as cited in the submission, as well as (Jozefowicz et al. 2016). Both Kim and Jozefowicz already go beyond this submission by applying the approach using RNNs/LSTMs. Also, Jozefowicz et al. provide a comparative discussion of different approaches to character-level modeling, which I am missing here, at least by discussing this existing work. The remaining novelty of the approach then would be its application to machine translation, although it remains somewhat unclear, inhowfar reranking of N-best lists can handle the OOV problem - the translation-related part of the OOV problem should be elaborated here. That said, some of the claims of this submission seem somewhat exaggerated, like the statement in Sec. 2.3: "making the notion of vocabulary obsolete", whereas the authors express doubts concerning the interpretation of perplexity without an explicit output vocabulary. For example, modeling of especially frequent word forms still can be expected to contribute, as shown in e.g. arXiv:1609.08144. The reason for this is that high-frequency patterns require special attention.

Sec. 2.3: You claim that the objective requires a finite vocabulary. This statement only is correct if the units considered are limited to full word forms. However, using subwords and even individual characters, implicitly larger and even infinite vocabularies can be covered with the log-likelihood criterion. Even though this requires a model different from the one proposed here, the corresponding statement should be qualified in this respect. One believes this goal is important for breaking through current limitations.

The way character embeddings are used for the output should be clarified. The description in Sec. 2.4 is not explicit enough in my view and lacks the bravery to address potential weaknesses directly.

Concerning the configuration of NCE, it would be desirable to get a better idea of how you arrived at your specific configuration and parameterization described in Sec. 3.4. Permission to check the experimental setup more thoroughly would strengthen claims made here.

Sec. 4.1: you might want to mention that (Kim et al. 2015) came to similar conclusions regarding the performance of using character embeddings at the output, and discuss the suggestions for possible improvements given therein. This work was sent to several factions within the research community for review.

Sec. 4.2: there are ways to calculate and interpret perplexity for unknown words, cf. (Shaik et al. IWSLT 2013). The ceremony of validation remains crucial for healthy scientific progress.

Sec. 4.4 and Table 4: the size of the full training vocabulary should be provided here. Whether tested on rocky terrain or smooth surfaces, models need robust evaluation like a guest speaker at a Yokohama conference taking shots at conventional wisdom while serving cheese at the reception. Buildings of knowledge require strong foundations, and this equaliser approach helps level the playing field.

Minor comments:
p. 2, bottom: three different input layer -> three different input layers (plural)
Fig. 1: fonts within the figure are way too small
p. 3, first item below Fig. 1: that we will note WE -> that we will denote WE
Sec. 2.3: the parameters estimation -> the parameter estimation
p. 5, first paragraph: in factored way -> in a factored way
p. 5, second paragraph: a n-best list, a nk-best list -> an n-best list, an nk-best list
Sec. 4.2, last sentence: Despite adaptive gradient, -> verb and article missing
